title: Open Rights Group raises concerns over Home Office AI asylum tools and calls for their suspension
description:
The Open Rights Group examined two AI tools used by the Home Office: the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS), tool which summarises asylum interview transcripts, and the Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, which helps caseworkers search country policy information.
As the report highlights, both AI tools generate their own new text rather than merely retrieving existing text and they can filter or omit facts relevant to a decision.
The Home Office is also not planning an independent audit of its AI tools and is not listing them on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Hub.
Responses to parliamentary questions and freedom of information (FOI) requests contained contradictory accounts of staff training and testing of the AI tools, the Open Rights Group said.
In addition, the Open Rights Group questioned whether the tools had delivered the efficiency improvements claimed by ministers.
text:
A new report by the Open Rights Group (ORG) has raised concerns about the Home Office's use of artificial intelligence (AI) in asylum decisions, with a six-month investigation highlighting significant error in content generated by AI tools and a lack of transparency and independent oversight.

The 20-page report can be downloaded here.

The Open Rights Group examined two AI tools used by the Home Office: the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS), tool which summarises asylum interview transcripts, and the Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, which helps caseworkers search country policy information. Both use OpenAI's GPT-4o model through Microsoft's Azure AI Foundry.

As the report highlights, both AI tools generate their own new text rather than merely retrieving existing text and they can filter or omit facts relevant to a decision.

A 2025 Home Office pilot evaluation found that 9% of ACS summaries were inaccurate or omitted information and had to be removed from the trial. However, subsequent sampling by Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) of 203 summaries after the tool's wider rollout found that 22% failed an initial assessment and 30 of 56 summaries examined at a second stage also failed.

Whilst noting that the exact SME procedures to test for a 'fail' were unclear, the Open Rights Group noted: "Therefore, across both stage reviews 22% and 15% of sampled summaries were assessed as not fit for use – significantly higher than the 9% figure in the Home Office's published pilot evaluation."

The Open Rights Group further notes that only 203 summaries were checked by Home Office SMEs between April and July 2026, representing only approximately 0.3% of the estimated 70,000 cases processed during that period.

According to the report, the situation for the APS tool is worse and there is no equivalent ongoing quality-control process. Anna Turley, the Minister of State for Border Security and Asylum, confirmed in August that the testing of the APS tool had now ceased.

The report further criticised the Home Office for not applying the UK Government's AI Playbook to the tools, which offers guidance on using AI safely, effectively and securely. The Home Office is also not planning an independent audit of its AI tools and is not listing them on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Hub.

Responses to parliamentary questions and freedom of information (FOI) requests contained contradictory accounts of staff training and testing of the AI tools, the Open Rights Group said. Some FOI requests were refused.

The report states: "The Home Office has refused to provide key information including about staff training, the prompts being used, and how the tools are being tested for quality assurance. Their replies have been at times self-contradictory. Our findings suggest that these tools have been rolled out without proper testing, quality assurance and training. This careless approach could have catastrophic consequences for those people whose future is in the hands of Home Office decision-making."

In addition, the Open Rights Group questioned whether the tools had delivered the efficiency improvements claimed by ministers. Its analysis of Home Office data found that the average monthly number of initial substantive asylum decisions since April 2026 had fallen by about 42% compared with the same period in 2025, while the mean time between substantive interview and decision had increased by 29%.

The report calls on the Home Office to suspend both tools, commission an independent evaluation and audit, and ask the Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration to investigate their use.

It says there should be no use of AI in the asylum decision-making process without proper consultation, adherence to domestic regulations and international obligations, and full alignment with human rights principles

text:
Attorneys for the US government and a Dominican woman fighting her removal from the country struggled to convince the full Third Circuit on whether the court has any role to play in the case.

Several judges pressed the Justice Department’s Drew Ensign during en banc oral argument Wednesday on his position that the reinstated removal order was merely “ministerial,” and judicial review is explicitly barred by the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Judge Cheryl Ann Krause sought to poke holes in that characterization, posing a hypothetical about what a US citizen with the same name as a removed individual would do if faced with a reinstatement order that under the government’s position would not be reviewable.

Judge Patty Shwartz also pushed Ensign, who leads the DOJ Civil Division’s Office of Immigration Litigation, to explain his position on reinstatement orders. Shwartz previously authored the majority opinion for a divided three-judge panel in the case, ruling that the court has jurisdiction to review the Board of Immigration Appeal’s denial of relief under the Convention Against Torture, but affirming the BIA’s denial.

Other judges — including Chief Judge Michael Chagares, Judge Jennifer Mascott, and Judge Peter Phipps — questioned David Zimmer of Zimmer, Citron & Clarke LLP, who represents the woman seeking immigration relief, about whether the text of the statute allows for judicial review of reinstatement orders.

There’s no dispute the court can’t review the prior order of removal, Zimmer told the judges, but nothing says it can’t review the reinstatement order. A reinstatement order is a reviewable final order of removal because it’s the mechanism by which a past removal order may be implemented, Zimmer said.

Patria Laureano, a citizen of the Dominican Republic, was arrested in 2023 for having unlawfully reentered the United States following a removal order. Laureano first entered the US in 1994 and while in the US was physically abused by her partner. He sent a package containing drugs to her workplace in 2005, and when Laureano was arrested and subsequently cooperated with law enforcement, he threatened to kill her.

Laureano pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute one kilogram or more of heroin and served a two-year sentence, then was ordered removed to the Dominican Republic in 2008. The removal order was reinstated when she was arrested in 2023. Laureano sought relief on the basis that her former partner, who now resides in the Dominican Republic, could harm her if she returned, and the Dominican police wouldn’t protect her.

An immigration judge denied her application, and the Board of Immigration Appeals adopted that decision in full, dismissing Laureano’s appeal. The judge found that she hadn’t met the standard for CAT relief because she failed to show that her former partner would seriously harm her if she returned to the Dominican Republic and that Dominican officials wouldn’t take action to protect her. Laureano then asked the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit to review the ruling.

Legal Services of New Jersey also represents Laureano.

The case is Laureano v. Attorney General, 3d Cir. en banc, No. 24-02433, oral argument 10/14/26.

title: On Immigration, Common Ground May Be Closer Than We Think - The Fulcrum
description:
As Americans read the names of people killed 25 years ago, families elsewhere were mourning loved ones killed in wars today.
The Moral Distance Families grieve their own differently from strangers.
Emotional distance is understandable, but it can also become moral distance.
Our national wealth, geographic security, and military superiority have insulated most Americans from the consequences of wars fought in our name.
My Own Moral Distance I know something about the insulation I am describing.
text:
I found it deeply moving. Time has not diminished the grief, the courage, or the human cost of that day.

I think about the firefighters.

While thousands of people were desperately trying to get out of the World Trade Center, firefighters were going in. One of them was Battalion Chief Orio Palmer.

Palmer took an elevator to the 41st floor of the South Tower and then climbed 37 flights carrying roughly 50 pounds of equipment. He reached the devastated 78th-floor sky lobby, moving toward trapped civilians. The 9/11 Commission Report records that firefighters freed civilians trapped in an elevator shortly before the tower collapsed. Palmer did not make it out.

He did not know the people he was climbing toward, only that they were in danger. We rightly remember that as heroism.

But as I watched the commemorations, another thought kept intruding.

People are also dying violently elsewhere as I write this, in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran. Behind us are Afghanistan, Iraq and other wars.

As Americans read the names of people killed 25 years ago, families elsewhere were mourning loved ones killed in wars today.

We remember our dead by name. We can remember theirs only by numbers.

The Moral Distance

Families grieve their own differently from strangers. Communities and nations preserve their own tragedies. No human being can feel every death in the world with the intensity of losing a spouse, a child, or a friend. Our concern naturally begins close to home.

Emotional distance is understandable, but it can also become moral distance.

This human tendency is not uniquely American. But for the United States, it operates alongside extraordinary power. American military forces can reach almost anywhere on Earth. Our national wealth, geographic security, and military superiority have insulated most Americans from the consequences of wars fought in our name.

Our cities stay intact. Our lights stay on. Our children go to school. We know war mostly through reports, not through lived experience.

For much of our recent history, war has happened somewhere else. September 11 was the exception. For a few hours, the distance collapsed. Nearly 3,000. We know the names behind that number.

Names Are Buried In Numbers

Brown University’s Costs of War project estimates that more than 940,000 people died directly from post-9/11 war violence in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen, and Pakistan between 2001 and 2023. When indirect deaths from war’s damage to health systems and infrastructure are included, the project estimates at least 4.5 million deaths.

Many actors caused those deaths in very different conflicts. They are not a count of people killed by the United States. Deliberately murdering civilians, military action against legitimate targets, strategic error, and unintended civilian deaths carry very different moral and legal responsibilities.

But numbers this large tell us almost nothing about the people behind them. Distance does not make those lives less human.

One of them was Hami.

Hami was 11. He loved soccer and riding his bicycle. On February 28, his grandfather, Heydar Sadeghi, drove Hami, his 9-year-old sister Nila, and their mother, Neda Salehizadeh, a teacher, to their school in Minab, Iran. He planned to pick them up at 1 p.m.

At least one U.S. missile struck the school that morning, according to an Associated Press investigation. Hami and his mother were killed. Nila was pulled alive from the rubble. When Sadeghi reached the school, he searched through the destruction, calling their names.

One important fact should not be pushed aside. The school stood next to a compound operated by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Some of its students were children of officers at the base. Many were local children from Minab.

The circumstances of the strike and the Guard compound matter. So do questions of military necessity, intent, and responsibility. U.S. military investigators reached a preliminary assessment that American forces were likely responsible, although the investigation had not reached a final conclusion when Reuters reported on it.

None of that makes Hami less human.

The number is how we encounter the death. His name is how Hami’s grandfather remembers him.

My Own Moral Distance

I know something about the insulation I am describing.

Around 1980, part of my professional work involved analyzing the impacts of Agent Orange from U.S. military use during the Vietnam War. The analysis included what had happened in Vietnamese villages: studies, exposure information, impacts, and numbers.

That was how I saw it then: numbers and facts. I did not stop to ask about the people inside those numbers. That was my insulation.

I am asking the question now as I experience 9/11’s 25th anniversary.

What “Never Forget” Asks of Us

For 25 years, “Never Forget” has been a promise.

We should remember who died, what was endured, and the courage and sacrifice. We should preserve the story so later generations understand what happened that morning.

But remembrance carries an obligation forward as well.

If remembering only preserves our own wound, its moral reach remains limited. The intimacy with which we understand the suffering of September 11 can help us grasp what violent death does to a family anywhere.

We need not feel guilt for everything done in our country’s name. But we should ask what price was paid, what proved wrong, what humanity was lost, and what was easier to overlook because it happened far away.

Remembrance should enlarge our moral imagination. It should take what we learned from our own suffering and change how we see the suffering of people we do not know.

Moral imagination should guide how we use that power.

Sometimes military force may be necessary. But a country with our reach and power should be especially careful about using it. Those who bear the consequences usually live far from us, and distance makes them easier to ignore.

America’s power places a greater responsibility on us. When we can use force without experiencing its consequences ourselves, we have an obligation to understand what those consequences mean before we act.

The question is whether we clearly see the people who may pay the price before we decide to use force.

The People Who Ran In

Orio Palmer climbed the stairs.

He moved toward strangers. He did not need their names to decide their lives mattered.

We cannot know every name in every war. We cannot grieve every loss as we grieve our own. But we should not confuse distance with insignificance.

Orio Palmer had a name.

Hami had a name.

Twenty-five years ago, firefighters entered burning buildings to reach people whose names they did not know. Remembering those we lost that day is where “Never Forget” begins.

For me now, “Never Forget” also means seeing the names inside the numbers when our power puts distant lives in our hands.

-----

Edward Saltzberg is the Executive Director of the Security and Sustainability Forum and a Visiting Scholar at George Washington University. He writes the Substack, The Stability Brief.

Across the country, Americans are searching for ways to survive the noise — corruption, turbulence, and dysfunction. They are navigating an affordability crisis dismissed as a “hoax,” a healthcare system buckling under pressure, a measles outbreak, and rising global instability, including the Iran war. They are watching unqualified people confirmed to positions of national importance while an election-denying president dominates the news cycle, abuses the office, and evades accountability. They see institutions strained, rights challenged, and democratic norms tested. Many are simply trying to hold on — to their peace, their sanity, their hope.

And in the middle of all this, Americans turn toward one another — toward kindness, community, faith, humor, and resilience — because that is where real care still exists. In the absence of compassion from the top, they make the most of what they have.

But chaos is not the whole story. Noise is not destiny. And noise is not who we are. Through it all, Americans continue to rise. I saw that resilience on 9/11. Living in California, my husband — who worked in aerospace — narrowly missed his flight to New York. My cousin’s subway train in Manhattan stalled underground. One of my Muslim teachers told me her husband did not want her to come to work because he feared she would be mistreated. She said, “My principal values diversity — she will keep me safe,” and she came anyway. My niece in northern Virginia watched military planes fly overhead. In those hours, Americans of every background prayed together, comforted one another, and showed extraordinary courage. I remember asking my entire school to pause for a moment of silence. Even in unimaginable grief, America rose.

Hard times do something unexpected: they make love stronger. Couples hold each other closer. Friends become anchors. Communities tighten their circles. Look at the neighborhoods surrounding Haitian families and other immigrants — people who came to America, built lives, contributed to their communities, and helped make those communities stronger, only to find themselves facing fear, uncertainty, and political hostility. Yet communities stepped in. Neighbors share food. Families donate to food banks even when their own budgets are thin. People with almost nothing find ways to give. My mother used to say, “You can’t miss what you have never had.” And she was right. Americans know what it means to depend on one another. They rise through empathy, connection, sacrifice, and love.

There is also a striking contradiction. The president is the son of an immigrant, and he has married two immigrant women: his late first wife, Ivana Trump, who was born in Czechoslovakia, and his current wife, Melania Trump, who was born in Slovenia and became a naturalized U.S. citizen. Both are white European immigrants. Yet Haitian and other immigrants of color can find themselves facing fear, uncertainty, and political hostility. America is not strengthened by deciding who is worthy of belonging. It is strengthened when people see one another as human beings worthy of dignity.

Just today, my nephew sent me pictures and videos from Symphony in the Park in Atlanta — a huge crowd of diverse people gathered under the open sky. “Everybody is here,” he said. And he was right. People of every background were talking, laughing, sharing food, and enjoying the evening together. Strangers spoke with strangers. Families relaxed side by side. Here they were, choosing joy over noise, community over cruelty, and connection over division.

Even now, Americans continue to show quiet acts of goodness. My sister in Virginia found herself part of a “pay it forward” chain at Walmart. I experienced it myself in a fast-food drive-through — someone paid for my order. I watched a man in a grocery store hand a woman two dollars when she was short on her bill. “Take the $1.67 and keep the change,” he said. No politics. No division. Just humanity.

A grieving mother adopted a five-year-old girl her late daughter had planned to adopt, carrying forward her daughter’s love. A waitress patiently read a menu to a confused customer, restoring their dignity. An older man paid for another person’s groceries and simply said, “Been there, kid.” These moments are not small. They are evidence of who we are.

America may feel far from the country many of us remember. This administration has cast a cloud over that spirit — a cloud of cruelty, division, intimidation, and corruption. But resilience remains the quiet force holding this country together. Americans are struggling to endure an affordability crisis and a political crisis at the same time. Yet they smile. They rise.

My mother taught my siblings and me something simple that stayed with me throughout my life: Don’t look down. Keep your head up. Look toward the heavens and smile.

I did just that.

Years later, I had a supervisor whose tactics seemed designed to break people. I watched adults under his supervision cry, quit, give in, or become loyal to him simply to survive. He once asked me why I was always smiling. He told me people were suspicious of me because I was always smiling.

I looked at him, smiled, and walked away.

He could not break me. He did everything he could to keep me from being promoted, but his tactics did not work. Thank goodness I had learned something long before I entered that workplace: another person does not get to decide whether I surrender my spirit.

People need to remember that inner strength now. Resilience is not pretending hardship does not hurt. It is knowing that hardship does not have to define you. Sometimes strength is simply keeping your head up, looking toward the light, and refusing to let someone else take your joy.

Do not give in to the noise. Weed through lies and conspiracies. Do your research. Seek the truth. Remember the past, especially when leaders claim they “did right by you.” Make a plan to vote. And vote.

Don’t get sidelined by party loyalty, election interference, or intimidation. Protect your voice. Protect your power. Protect the Republic.

Protect something else, too: your inner strength. Step away from the noise when you need to. Look up. Smile. Breathe. Stay connected to people who remind you of hope and possibility. Believe that your effort matters.

My mother used to say, “No one can take your joy. You can give it away, but no one can take it.”

She was right.

We may not be able to control every storm around us. But we can decide whether we will surrender our humanity, our hope, our voice, or our joy to it.

America’s quiet strength has always lived in its people.

And still, we rise.

Carolyn Goode is a retired educational leader and former principal who has spent her career advancing civic responsibility, equity, and public engagement. She writes about democracy, leadership, and the values that strengthen American communities.

description:
The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA) represent the labor unions.
Since taking power, the Trump administration has created a mass surveillance program to monitor constitutionally protected speech by noncitizens lawfully present in the U.S.
In October 2025, UAW, CWA, and AFT sued the Departments of State and Homeland Security, alleging that this viewpoint-based surveillance program violates the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act.
"Our plaintiff-unions have members that have wholly changed the way they interact with social media—including limiting their engagement with union content—because of the government's social media surveillance program," said EFF Senior Staff Attorney Lisa Femia.

text:
A lawsuit filed by three labor unions against the Departments of State and Homeland Security for their viewpoint-based surveillance and suppression of protected expression online can move forward, a federal judge ruled earlier this month.

On October 1, 2026, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York rejected the government’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit. The case was filed in October 2025 on behalf of the United Automobile Workers (UAW), Communications Workers of America (CWA), and American Federation of Teachers (AFT). The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA) represent the labor unions.

This decision is a victory: The Court held that claims that the government’s social media surveillance program is harming the unions’ members, as well as hampering the ability of the unions to associate with their members and potential members, can move forward.

The Court ruled that: "This threat of adverse immigration consequences, under a government whose harsh immigration crackdowns has been heavily publicized and reported on, is certainly enough to 'deter a person of ordinary firmness from the exercise of First Amendment rights.' It is objectively reasonable that noncitizens would limit their expression of disfavored viewpoints under the [Challenged Surveillance Program] given the credible threat of adverse immigration action from the Government."

Since taking power, the Trump administration has created a mass surveillance program to monitor constitutionally protected speech by noncitizens lawfully present in the U.S. Using AI and other automated technologies, the program surveils the social media accounts of visa and green card holders with the goal of identifying and punishing those who express viewpoints the government disfavors. The surveillance program has been paired with a public intimidation campaign—silencing not just noncitizens with immigration status, but also the families, coworkers, and friends with whom their lives are integrated.

In October 2025, UAW, CWA, and AFT sued the Departments of State and Homeland Security, alleging that this viewpoint-based surveillance program violates the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act.

"Our plaintiff-unions have members that have wholly changed the way they interact with social media—including limiting their engagement with union content—because of the government's social media surveillance program," said EFF Senior Staff Attorney Lisa Femia. "Many have stopped posting online together, and have even stopped engaging in offline activities, for fear of being scrutinized or targeted related to immigration benefits. We are pleased that the Court has agreed to let the case proceed, and allow unions and their members to seek justice for infringement of their rights."

READ MORE…

🎃 OPT OUT OCTOBER: Big tech companies are hell-bent on taking away our agency and forcing us to use their surveillance-based services, apps, and devices. But with a little work, we can stand our ground and take control over what happens with our data. This month—Opt Out October—we’re walking through some of the steps to do just that. Begin your Opt Out October journey today with our guides for opting out of social media, software, and AI tools made by Big Tech.

😎 VPN VICTORY: When lawmakers try to rewrite how the internet works, users rely on courts to recognize that laws can’t make technical impossibilities a reality. That’s why we were happy to see that a court has blocked Utah’s attempt to outlaw the privacy protections of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs). In a win for digital rights, a federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking Utah’s SB 73, the state’s draconian anti-VPN age verification law. The decision comes as EFF submitted our comments to the Utah Department of Commerce, detailing how forcing platforms to detect and block privacy-preserving tools undermines user privacy and security worldwide while demanding the impossible.

🪪 NO ID, NO INTERNET?: Online age verification proposals are often presented as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children on the internet. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? Age verification laws that are predicated on users possessing identity documents exclude critical sections of populations. And this problem is global in nature: Millions of people lack government-issued identification or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it.

🤐 COPYRIGHT TROLLS: Whether Congress calls it SOPA, PIPA, ACPA, or the DEFEND IP Act, every site-blocking bill has the same rotten idea at their core: That enforcing copyrights requires building a censorship machine for websites into the architecture of the internet. This is, of course, a disaster for a free and open web. These proposals keep coming, but there is still no way to create a mechanism for blocking access to an entire website that does not invite both deliberate abuse and lots of collateral harm to free and lawful speech.

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, and her Republican challenger Chris Shea squared off in a Tuesday night debate that featured contrasting views and occasional sharp exchanges over Trump administration policies, immigration and the war in Iran. The forum hosted by the League of Women Voters of Litchfield County was the first and likely only debate between Hayes and Shea ahead of the Nov. 3 election. They are running for Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District, which remains one of the state’s only competitive races for federal office. One of the biggest contrasts between the candidates during the debate was over H.R. 1, Republicans’ party-line tax legislation that passed last year and was dubbed by President Donald Trump as the “big beautiful bill.” Hayes said she would prioritize trying to rescind some of the cuts to programs like Medicaid and the federal nutrition program known as SNAP that the law will enact through changes to the programs like new work requirements. Nearly 63,000 residents in Connecticut already lost SNAP benefits since eligibility rules changed as a result of H.R. 1. Shea, on the other hand, said he wants to see the bill’s tax relief measures strengthened or made permanent. He noted his opponent’s opposition to the bill, which also included new federal deductions for overtime pay or tips, as well as an increase on the cap for state and local tax (SALT) deductions. Hayes said she supports tax relief provisions like those, but noted that many of them expire in 2028 when Trump’s term ends. She called those temporary tax breaks “crumbs on the table,” while wealthier people and corporations benefit from permanent tax cuts. The two candidates also disagreed over the authority of the executive and the legislative branches in relation to the president’s tariff agenda and a war in Iran that has stretched into its eighth month. On tariffs, Shea acknowledged people in Connecticut and around the country have been affected in “multiple ways” and said he’s “not a fan either” of the higher costs of goods. But he defended Trump’s ability to impose tariffs by arguing that it can be helpful in negotiating trade deals and as a mechanism for spurring more manufacturing. “With tariffs, though, I think the thing that we need to look at is, as most things, we need to look at things eyes wide open,” Shea said. “And the executive branch and the State Department need to have tools to bargain with, and that’s one of them.” “But if he can’t use, or any administration can’t use that as a tool to negotiate with, I don’t think we’re putting them in the right position to negotiate on our behalf,” he said. Hayes pushed back, saying it’s the job of Congress to negotiate trade law, not the executive branch. She specifically cited the farmers in the 5th District who have been hurt by such policies, including higher costs that are a result of the war in the Middle East. “I don’t believe it’s the president’s prerogative to just wield tariffs as he pleases,” Hayes said. “The president should not have the power to unilaterally impose tariffs on behalf of our nation.” “I want to go back to Congress so that we can put a check on this administration so that we can make sure we are doing the will of the people, not the will of the president,” she added. The candidates also debated the ongoing war with Iran, which led to a back-and-forth over which branch of government holds the authority to engage in war. They were specifically asked how Congress can ensure the administration seeks congressional authorization before ordering more military strikes. Shea, who served as a Navy SEAL for more than three decades, said he “vehemently disagrees” with the characterization that military action against Iran was a war of choice, arguing that Iran continues to pose a threat to the U.S. “If we’re going to go to full war with them, then yeah, Congress has to authorize it. That’s what the rules are,” Shea said. “But the president is the commander-in-chief and has the ability to make decisions based on intelligence that is timely and get after those target sets that are necessary.” Hayes said she’s already voted five times in the House for war powers resolutions that would rein in military action until the president seeks congressional approval. She argued that Congress recessed early because House GOP leaders wanted to stop a vote on impeaching Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth — something Hayes said she supports. “Our Defense Department is on the wrong track, and Congress has to exert our oversight authorities and our Article 1 authorities,” she said. “This president is not a king.” The forum also touched on immigration policy, which comes at a fraught time in the 5th District given recent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in Danbury that led to the arrest of 118 people. While the Department of Homeland Security disputes it happened, video released by Danbury United for Immigrants on social media appears to show ICE officers arresting someone at a school bus stop. Both candidates agreed that Congress needs to tackle more comprehensive immigration reform and border security, but their views diverged from there. Hayes called the current policies surrounding deportations and ICE “lawlessness,” and noted that it’s “peculiar” that Black and Brown communities are specifically targeted. She pointed to the recent decision to end Temporary Protected Status that was affirmed over the summer by the U.S. Supreme Court. Shea appeared to take issue with Connecticut’s Trust Act, arguing the state has “gone in the wrong direction with interfering in federal law enforcement.” “I think the cases that the congresswoman brought up of people being grabbed in less than desirable locations is a forcing function of what the government here has done,” Shea said. “The safest place for someone to get detained by ICE is in a courtroom, is in a jail, is in one of these public places, not in neighborhoods, not in churches.” While they ultimately disagreed on most issues, there were a few areas of agreement. On data centers, Hayes said the companies need to “pay their fair share” when it comes to the energy these large facilities consume and that Congress should consider federal oversight. Shea largely agreed with the need for oversight, saying that local zoning needs to be respected while also noting that the U.S. remains in an artificial intelligence race with China. The candidates were also asked how they envision their priorities and committee work in the next session of Congress. Shea said he’d like to serve on a committee with jurisdiction over veterans and defense issues. He also signaled interest regarding agriculture. Hayes hopes to continue serving on her current assignments: the House Agriculture Committee and the House Education and Workforce Committee. She recently announced she will run for the top spot on the latter, facing a few other Democrats. “I plan to run as chairman of this committee because I will not sit in Congress and do nothing while the doors of the Department of Education close,” Hayes said, citing both her work on education and labor issues. She used that moment in the debate to take a jab at her opponent, pointing out that “Shea’s own union didn’t even endorse him,” referring to her endorsement from the Uniformed Professional Fire Fighters Association of Connecticut. Shea works as a firefighter in North Haven. He appeared unbothered by the union’s endorsement of the congresswoman. “It’s like calling the sky blue. The union endorsed the Democrats — surprise, surprise,” Shea said. “The boys will be voting for me.” Hayes is seeking a fifth term to represent the sprawling district in the western part of the state, which is viewed as the most competitive congressional race in Connecticut. In addition to his work as a firefighter and a Navy SEAL, Shea founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders. Hayes, a former teacher who won National Teacher of the Year in 2016, faced Republican George Logan in her last two reelection races. Both received national attention and resources but her 2024 race was not as close as the one in 2022. The district is viewed as Connecticut’s most competitive congressional race. But this cycle, election analysts who rate federal races moved Connecticut’s 5th District closer to Democrats. And historically, the party in power faces headwinds in a midterm election. The League of Women Voters’ forum comes less than a week before in-person early voting, which begins Oct. 19 and runs through Nov. 1. Voters can also vote absentee by mail; The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2. Those ballots must arrive before polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day.

description:
Prior to the investigation, multiple Trump Administration officials have accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting any evidence.
Stripping someone of their citizenship is a more arduous legal process than most other immigration efforts that involve the courts.
The denaturalization process, on the other hand, must be approved by an independent federal judge, who evaluates the request by a higher standard.
The allegations regarding Omar’s citizenship gained attention among conservative activists and commentators starting in 2019, when Omar became a member of Congress.
Despite the renewed push from the second Trump administration, denaturalization remains an exceedingly rare legal process.
text:
In a highly unusual step, federal agents this week aggressively intensified their investigations into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, weeks before she stands for reelection in her home district.

The Department of Justice on Tuesday subpoenaed relatives of Omar’s family members, including her sister Sahra Noor, according to The New York Times. The grand jury subpoenas were issued shortly after a raid of the lawmaker’s residence in Washington, D.C. on Monday.

The judicial search warrant, which is under seal, was executed by Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Although the Department of Justice did not provide any more details of the investigation, multiple outlets, citing anonymous sources, reported that the search stemmed from Omar’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.

Prior to the investigation, multiple Trump Administration officials have accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting any evidence. In a podcast interview in March, Vice President JD Vance said the White House was exploring “legal remedies” to her alleged immigration fraud. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the investigation into Omar was “ongoing” and dismissed efforts to frame the case as political retribution.

“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said during the interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson.

Omar, who has long denied the allegations, condemned the raid on her home as “political intimidation” and said she will “not be silenced.”

President Trump, along with many MAGA Republicans, has repeatedly floated the idea of revoking Omar’s citizenship, a process also known as denaturalization, and deporting her.

But legal and immigration experts tell TIME that denaturalizing a U.S. citizen is a rare and difficult process, one that requires federal authorities to clear a high bar in front of a federal judge. Here’s what to know about how the process works.

How does denaturalization work?

Stripping someone of their citizenship is a more arduous legal process than most other immigration efforts that involve the courts. Deportation proceedings, for instance, are initiated by ICE agents under the Department of Homeland Security and are then approved by immigration judges who are hired and work within the Department of Justice. The denaturalization process, on the other hand, must be approved by an independent federal judge, who evaluates the request by a higher standard.

All denaturalization efforts begin at DOJ. In order to revoke a naturalized person’s citizenship, a DOJ lawyer must decide whether to file a civil or a criminal petition in court. Yuripzy Morgan, an attorney and host of Free Range National podcase, said a civil complaint does not have a statute of limitation, whereas a criminal complaint has a statute of limitation of 10 years and must clear a much higher legal bar.

“For civil denaturalization, the government has to show that there is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the person in question obtained their naturalization either illegally, or they willfully misrepresented a material fact, ” Morgan says. She stressed that simply having an error in an immigration document doesn't mean that a judge is going to approve stripping a person of their citizenship.

For a criminal denaturalization conviction, the federal government must show “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that the individual knowingly obtained citizenship through fraud, which is the highest legal standard of proof required to secure a criminal conviction. In 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Maslenjak v. United States that only an illegal act that played a role in a person’s citizenship application could lead to criminal denaturalization, further narrowing down the scope of such efforts.

Omar’s father filled out and submitted her citizenship application on her behalf when she was 17. It is unclear what evidence, if any, the federal government has to show that anything in the application was fraudulent, or that Omar or her father intentionally misrepresented anything in that application.

Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a resident fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, pointed out that even after someone gets denaturalized, a deportation is not guaranteed. The person would still be able to retain their previous legal immigration status until a final order of removal is issued to the person by ICE.

“If they had a green card before they naturalized, even after they get denaturalized, they are going to have a green card,” Arthur says.

How did Rep. Omar get naturalized as a U.S. citizen?

According to Omar’s House biography, Omar and her family fled her home country Somalia when she was eight. The family eventually sought asylum in the United States in 1995. She told The New York Times that she became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17.

At the time Omar went through the process, federal law allowed immigrants under the age of 18 to get naturalized as U.S. citizens if both of their parents had become U.S. citizens. The law was eventually replaced by a new law in 2001, which only requires one parent to become a citizen for the children to be naturalized.

At the center of this investigation is whether Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied about her age in immigration documents so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him, according to The Washington Post, which cited two unnamed sources.

According to Arthur, the former immigration judge, if Omar was 18 at the time of the naturalization application, she may have been able to apply for her citizenship on her own after having a valid green card for five years.

The allegations regarding Omar’s citizenship gained attention among conservative activists and commentators starting in 2019, when Omar became a member of Congress. Shortly after her election, Omar’s staff sought to change her official birth year in public records from 1981 to 1982, according to multiple outlets.

Despite the renewed push from the second Trump administration, denaturalization remains an exceedingly rare legal process. According to the Migration Policy Institute, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, an average of 11 denaturalization cases were filed per year between 1990 and 2017.

Denaturalization efforts have increased in Trump’s second term. The DOJ has announced efforts to strip at least 108 people of their citizenship in 2026. That is still considerably smaller than the hundreds of thousands of people whom the U.S. government grants citizenship to through naturalization every year.

text:
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said this week that his office will investigate why an immigration agent driving an SUV ran over a 48-year-old man during an enforcement operation on Saturday.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said that ICE officers were searching for Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who had a deportation order, around 7:30 a.m. on Saturday.

ICE said that Miguel Parra-Hernandez was in the same vehicle as Mendoza-Cervantes, got out and ran in front of an ICE vehicle. But Kim Bruno, the attorney for Parra-Hernandez, said her client doesn’t know Mendoza-Cervantes and that he was not with him on Saturday.

“As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck,” according to a statement sent to The Texas Tribune on Saturday by TIm Oberle, a spokesperson for ICE in Houston.

Surveillance footage captured on a nearby camera depicts two men getting out of a white pickup truck and running in different directions through a parking lot. The footage also shows a black SUV pursue one of the men from behind as he ran from it. Teare said in an interview with KTRK-TV that he believes the ICE agent intentionally hit Parra-Hernandez. He added that “a charging decision is going to come in a relatively short order in this case.”

“ICE tactics are growing more brazen and more dangerous,” Teare said in a statement. “High-speed pursuits and aggressive operations on busy streets put everyone at risk. No badge puts anyone above the law in Harris County and we will continue to follow evidence wherever it may lead.”

Mendoza-Cervantes, who ICE said has been previously arrested in connection to driving under the influence and unlawful possession of a firearm, fled on foot. As of Tuesday, federal agents were looking for him, ICE said in a statement.

“Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are reckless and false,” ICE said in the email.

At a news conference on Sunday, family members and immigrant rights advocates with the group FIEL said Parra-Hernandez was on his way to work.

“We want justice,” Rodolfo Parra, the man’s brother, said at the news conference. They said that Parra-Hernandez suffered two broken legs and underwent surgery. As of Monday, he was recovering at a hospital in Katy.

Natxielly Castañeda, Parra-Hernandez’s niece, said at the news conference that her uncle most likely ran from ICE out of fear, especially because he has lived in the U.S. for nearly 30 years without being in trouble with the law.

“We’re not animals, we shouldn’t be treated the way we’re being treated right now,” she said.

Bruno told the Houston Chronicle she is working to release her client from ICE custody.

ICE tactics questioned

The incident comes after another ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, in July as he was driving to a job site with his employees in Houston. In a more recent incident in Austin, an ICE agent shot and injured 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez on Sept. 20 as he was working as a DoorDash food delivery driver. Prosecutors in Harris and Travis counties are also investigating these shootings.

ICE has come under public scrutiny for a spate of fatal and non-fatal shootings since the Trump administration returned to office. President Trump has prioritized immigration enforcement throughout the country, claiming that immigration agents are targeting previously convicted criminals who can be deported. Other news publications have reported the Trump administration has set a target of 3,000 daily arrests as part of Trump’s mass deportation efforts.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, a former U.S. Department of Homeland Security official during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, said the pressure of meeting a daily quota and cutting down on ICE training have resulted in some deportation officers using more force.

“We are seeing more of these — what I would call extreme reactions — to try to get an arrest. Where in the past agents would have said, ‘Never mind, it’s not that important. We’re not going to endanger ourselves or somebody else to get this arrest,’” said Cardinal Brown, who is now an adviser for the Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C., think tank.

Advocates and some Democratic lawmakers have blasted the Trump administration, saying ICE’s aggressive tactics are putting the general public’s safety at risk.

“Having an ICE badge and being an undercover agent does not give anybody license to treat people this way,” said Cesar Espinosa with FIEL at the Sunday news conference.

Lauren Bonds, executive director of the National Police Accountability Project, said in a statement that local officials need to investigate ICE’s use-of-force cases to determine whether federal agents were justified. She added that Congress also needs to rein in ICE to prevent further violence.

“The tactics ICE is using — car chases, ramming vehicles, and shooting people who pose no threat to the public — are dangerous and illegal when local police use them and they are dangerous and illegal when ICE uses them. No one — man, woman, or child — deserves to die from these brutal tactics.”

Congress to investigate ICE shootings

In previous ICE shootings, DHS has released preliminary information that was later contradicted by video footage or witness statements.

For example, in Salgado Araujo’s case, DHS initially said that he tried to ram ICE vehicles. But the other three men in the van later said Salgado Araujo never tried to hit the officers. Instead, they said ICE vehicles struck them from behind and the side before one of the agents fired, striking Salgado Araujo in the stomach.

“We need to know exactly what happened, and ICE’s word alone is not enough,” U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, D-Houston, said in a statement posted on social media. “ICE has lied to the public before, and its operations have brought chaos to our communities.”

On Thursday, U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, and Garcia will join other lawmakers at a congressional field hearing in Austin to get more information about ICE shootings in Texas.

The witnesses include Rachel Reyes, the mother of Ruben Ray Martinez, who was fatally shot by an ICE agent in 2025; and Kristen Etter, a lawyer for Garces Perez and an attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union in Texas.

text:
(NATCHEZ, MS) – Today, Rep. Bennie G. Thompson (D-MS), Ranking Member of the Committee on Homeland Security, and Rep. Troy Carter (D-LA), Committee Member, released the below statement on their surprise oversight visit yesterday to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility at Adams County Correctional Center (ACCC) in Mississippi, the nation’s largest migrant detention facility.

“One of Congress’ primary responsibilities is oversight of federal agencies, and we exercised that power – and legal right – in an unannounced visit to ACCC after a summer of crises, protests, and power outages. We wanted an unvarnished look at the institution to make sure that facility problems highlighted in correspondence our offices and in public inspection reports are being addressed, and that everyone in the facility has access to their constitutional due process rights. Regardless of a person’s station in life, they are still human and deserve safe shelter with adequate, sanitary food and water, and access to health care.

“We continue to have concerns that detainees aren’t able to obtain access to adequate mental health services, a full understanding of what crimes they are charged with, and transparency and accountability for when ACCC staff fail in upholding their constitutional rights. As the Trump administration continues to weaponize ICE against communities across the country, we will continue rigorous oversight of immigrant detention facilities so that the law is followed and immigrants have access to their full constitutional rights.”

Background:

Adams County Correctional Center (ACCC), operated by the private prison company CoreCivic, is the largest permanent immigration detention facility in the U.S. and detains an average of 1,878 men daily.

In the past six months, ACCC and the men detained there have experienced multiple crises. In May 2026, ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight inspected ACCC and downgraded the facility from a “Superior” rating to “Acceptable/Adequate,” with only 24 of 28 standards met. In July, nearly 70 detainees submitted a petition to the warden demanding an end to the practice of placing three detainees in cells meant to hold two people. During the week of August 10, 2026, a lengthy power outage at ACCC left detainees without air conditioning for two days in nearly 100-degree heat. On August 22, 2026, around 100 male detainees started a protest over poor living conditions, spoiled food, and meager rations.

text:
The heads of the main U.S. evangelical umbrella body and the Catholic bishops' migration committee have issued a joint statement urging Congress to open legal pathways for longtime immigrant residents, while affirming that the government has a duty to secure the country's borders.

The statement, "A Call for Christian Compassion and Wisdom in the Immigration Debate," was released Wednesday (Oct. 14) by the co-chairs of the Evangelical-Catholic Dialogue on Immigration, Rev. Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, and Bishop Brendan Cahill of Victoria, Texas, who chairs the Committee on Migration of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops.

Drawing on Scripture, the five-page document sets out three principles: human dignity, protection of the family and the proper role of government, and it argues that current U.S. enforcement practices have departed from them.

Its release follows a year in which the U.S. government sharply increased immigration arrests and deportations and nearly halted refugee admissions, while Christians in the United States remain divided over how to weigh border security against humanitarian obligations.

"As Catholic and evangelical Christians, we have doctrinal differences, but we are united in our conviction that God calls us to stand both with our fellow Americans who are experiencing economic and cultural anxieties and with our immigrant neighbors who are facing existential challenges," the two leaders wrote.

The NAE and the USCCB formed the dialogue in March 2026 to bring leaders of both traditions together on immigration, according to the NAE. Participants found broad agreement on the theological principles that should inform national policy, the association said.

Three principles based on the Old and New Testaments

The first principle rests on Genesis 1:27, which describes human beings as created in God's image. Before anyone is classified as a citizen or noncitizen, documented or undocumented, each person is a neighbor with "a claim on our conscience," the statement says.

"This dignity comes from God, not government, and no earthly power may erase it," it reads.

The authors cite Old Testament commands to love the foreigner, Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan and the story of Ruth the Moabite. They add that the same biblical obligations apply "with equal force" to U.S. citizens living in poverty, and they reject approaches that set citizens against noncitizens.

Family unity is the second principle, grounded in Genesis 2:24. The statement asserts that most people now facing detention and deportation in the United States are Catholic or evangelical Christians, and that roughly one in 12 Christians in the country either risks losing legal status or shares a home with someone who does.

Those figures come from "One Part of the Body," a March 2025 report by the USCCB's Migration and Refugee Services, the NAE, the evangelical relief agency World Relief and the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary. The report estimated that more than 10 million Christians were vulnerable to deportation at the end of 2024, about 80 percent of all those at risk. Catholics made up 61 percent of that group and evangelicals 13 percent, according to the report, which also found that nearly one in five U.S. Catholics was either at risk or living with someone who was.

"Their fear is our fear; their tears are ours to wipe," the co-chairs wrote.

The third principle, taken from Romans 13:1-7, affirms the government's responsibility to protect citizens and enforce "reasonable immigration policies." The document expresses gratitude for law enforcement officers and says many of them experience "moral injury when duty and conscience collide."

Even so, the co-chairs read the passage as describing authority that restrains wrongdoing. Directing enforcement at "the peaceful and productive majority" rather than at those who intend harm, they wrote, "is not an expression of Romans 13 but a departure from it."

Strengthening legal pathways

Both the executive branch and lawmakers bear responsibility, the statement says, but only Congress can correct what it calls "statutory shortcomings" in the legal immigration system. Existing routes to permanent status are "extremely limited and out of reach for most," the authors wrote, including for immigrants who have lived in the country for decades.

According to the document, majorities of evangelicals and Catholics favor reform that would allow longtime residents to regularize their status. A February 2025 Lifeway Research survey, sponsored in part by the NAE, found that 74 percent of self-identified evangelicals backed a path to citizenship for people in the country illegally who meet certain qualifications.

The co-chairs say reform legislation should also secure borders through "targeted, proportionate, and humane measures" that prioritize people who threaten public safety and respect due process.

They also call for strict limits on detaining nonviolent immigrants, especially children and families, with access to chaplains and legal counsel for everyone held. Legal routes for workers, family members and humanitarian migrants, they wrote, should be "safe, reliable, and efficient."

The leaders pledged to work with authorities so that every detainee, "of all faiths and none," can receive spiritual counsel and take part in the sacraments.

Enforcement and admissions figures

The statement itself does not cite enforcement statistics. Government data compiled by the Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research organization in Washington, D.C., indicate the scale of recent changes.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the federal agency responsible for arrests and removals inside the country, made about 236,000 administrative arrests in fiscal 2025, more than double the previous year's total, according to figures cited by the institute. MPI estimates that the agency carried out about 333,000 deportations over the same period.

Border encounters with migrants dropped to 692,000 in fiscal 2025. That compares with 2.9 million the year before and a record 3.2 million in fiscal 2023, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data reported by MPI.

The U.S. immigrant population reached a record 50.2 million in 2024, or 14.8 percent of residents, the institute reports. About 74 percent held legal status as of 2023, when MPI estimated the unauthorized population at roughly 13.7 million. Some 18.3 million children lived with at least one immigrant parent in 2024, and 85 percent of those children were born in the United States.

Refugee admissions have fallen to historic lows. The fiscal 2026 ceiling of 7,500 is the lowest since the modern resettlement program was created in 1980, and of the 3,158 refugees resettled in the first five months of that year, all but three came from South Africa, MPI reports.

Christian Daily International reported in September that World Relief and Open Doors US, in a report titled "State of the Golden Door," projected fiscal 2026 would likely be the first year in at least a quarter century in which no refugees facing religious persecution were resettled in the United States. The two Christian organizations said asylum approval rates in immigration court for applicants from the 50 countries on Open Doors' World Watch List fell to 10 percent in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, down from 58 percent in fiscal 2023.

The NAE-USCCB statement lists protecting the persecuted among the government's duties, alongside border security and upholding religious liberty.

The case for stricter enforcement

Support for the administration's approach remains strongest among white Christians. A Public Religion Research Institute survey released in March found that white evangelicals, at 69 percent, and white Catholics, at 53 percent, were the only religious groups in which a majority viewed President Donald Trump's handling of immigration favorably. Favorable views had declined in both groups, and in every other religious group surveyed, since March 2025.

The same survey found that 63 percent of white evangelicals and 55 percent of white Catholics agreed the federal government should hold immigrants in the country illegally in "internment camps" until they can be deported, compared with 41 percent of Americans overall. At the same time, 72 percent of Americans, including 55 percent of Republicans, said the United States should provide refuge to people who arrive facing serious danger in their home countries.

Those who favor stricter enforcement raise concerns the statement addresses only in part.

Many frame the issue as one of national sovereignty and the rule of law, arguing that a nation has the right to decide who enters and stays, and that failing to enforce existing law erodes public trust. The rise in border crossings that peaked in fiscal 2023 strained shelters and public services in several U.S. cities and became a central issue in the 2024 presidential election.

Critics of unauthorized immigration also argue that it is unfair to people who wait their turn. More than 4 million people were on the State Department's immigrant visa waiting list as of November 2023, according to MPI, and some family-based applications being processed in March 2026 had been filed in April 2001.

Public safety is another concern. Proponents of tougher enforcement point to crimes committed by people in the country illegally and argue those offenses could have been prevented by removal. The administration suspended Diversity Visa issuances in December 2025 and paused asylum decisions after fatal shootings allegedly carried out by noncitizens, MPI reports.

Economic effects are also debated. Some economists have argued that large inflows of lower-skilled workers depress wages for the native-born workers who compete most directly with them, particularly those without a high school diploma.

The case for expanding legal routes

Advocates for reform point to a legal system whose core limits have not changed in more than three decades. Annual caps of 226,000 family-sponsored and 140,000 employment-based green cards were set in 1990, and no single country may account for more than 7 percent of those visas, according to MPI. Nearly 946,000 approved employment-based petitions were awaiting an open visa slot as of June 2025.

Labor demand forms part of that argument. Immigrants and their U.S.-born children accounted for all growth in the prime working-age population since 2000 as birth rates declined, the institute reports.

Supporters of expanded legal migration, including the statement's authors, contend that wider legal channels would reduce irregular entry and free enforcement agencies to focus on public-safety threats.

Some who favor tighter limits counter that legalizing people already in the country could encourage future unauthorized migration. They point to the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act, which granted legal status to about 2.7 million people but was followed by rapid growth in the unauthorized population.

Resources for congregations

Immigration remains one of the most contested issues in U.S. public life, and the disagreements run through congregations as well as political parties. Christians who share convictions about human dignity and the authority of Scripture often reach different conclusions about how to weigh border security, the rule of law and obligations to the stranger.

In presenting the statement, the NAE pointed to “the complexity of the issue” and “the need for faithful engagement,” describing the document as a resource for churches, leaders and citizens.

It has proposed three ways for churches to use the statement. It encourages prayer for immigrants, policymakers and law enforcement officers, and suggests teaching the three biblical principles as a sermon series or small-group study.

The association also urges evangelicals to visit their members of Congress alongside a Catholic counterpart, or to write joint opinion pieces, as a sign of shared witness.

The statement links its appeal to the 250th anniversary of the U.S. Declaration of Independence, quoting its affirmation that all people are "endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights." The co-chairs committed to further education and dialogue within and between their traditions and invited local congregations to do the same.

"We do not offer these words in anger or partisanship but in hope, trusting that the God of the exile and the stranger has not abandoned his people," they wrote.

title: Pre-Election ICE Surge in California Could Backfire on Republicans
description:
A wave of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity against farmworkers in the Central Valley of California is upending one of the nation’s closest House races.
More from David Dayen In a swing district that’s 74 percent Latino, political disputes don’t get more controversial than this.
There are no specific numbers of detainees who have been taken, and according to the UFW, ICE has been slow-walking reporting of detentions to create obstacles to legal representation.
The timing of the surge, a month before the elections, could be designed to chill voter mobilization and balloting from Hispanic residents.
The UFW is continuing its registration and canvassing efforts, and officials believe the ICE raids will be top of mind for voters in the election.
text:
A wave of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity against farmworkers in the Central Valley of California is upending one of the nation’s closest House races. The raids in a major agricultural region with high concentrations of Latino farmworkers have taken dozens of community members into ICE custody over the past couple of weeks, spurring outrage and returning Donald Trump’s aggressive and unpopular immigration enforcement policies to the front pages, just as ballots arrived by mail.

“All law-abiding immigrants who work hard and contribute to our communities across the Central Valley have a right to go to work or drive their kids to school and return home safely,” said Randy Villegas, the progressive Democrat running in California’s 22nd Congressional District, in a statement. Villegas has continually criticized his opponent, incumbent Republican David Valadao, for voting to put $85 billion toward ICE’s enforcement budget and facilitating the mass arrests and deportations.

More from David Dayen

In a swing district that’s 74 percent Latino, political disputes don’t get more controversial than this. Valadao claimed last week that ICE told him the operation was “focused on individuals with active warrants and known criminal histories.” But locals with knowledge on the ground dispute that, saying that ICE is instead engaged in roving patrols designed to capture farmworkers as they head to the fields.

“Saying [raids] are targeted is not accurate,” said Elizabeth Strater, director of strategic campaigns for the United Farm Workers (UFW), which has reported ICE abductions in the Madera and Delano areas over the past week. “We call them suspicion-less stops, in the early morning on the roads of agricultural worksites. Regardless of status, regardless of having long-term work authorization, anybody that looks brown and working-class right now is being stopped.”

Agents conducting the ICE surge in California have reportedly been told to “go after anybody,” which supports the UFW’s account.

An unintentionally candid assessment of ICE’s roving patrols came out of Valadao’s mouth in a televised debate against Villegas last week. Asked about immigration enforcement, Valadao responded: “It is what it is.”

Ravi Mangla of the Working Families Party, which supports Villegas, responded: “Valadao made clear in the debate that he’s not going to stop or stand up to ICE, even when they terrorize his own constituents. He’s an absolute coward.”

STATE AND LOCAL MEDIA HAS REPORTED EXTENSIVELY on the sweeps, which have rounded up people who have spent as much as 49 years living in this country. According to residents and advocates, those detained were not asked for names or presented with warrants for their detentions. And while agricultural worksites have not been entered during the surge, locations have included public spaces outside Latino grocery stores, pharmacies, community hospitals, and even domestic violence shelters.

In April last year, a federal judge barred the Border Patrol from engaging in warrantless stops or roving patrols in California, but that order was set aside by an appeals court in August.

Some of the activity, like on rural roads in predawn hours, is designed to attract little attention from bystanders. This is consistent with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s efforts to engage in the same level of enforcement as under the showboating Kristi Noem, but in quieter ways with less public backlash.

One incident is emblematic, advocates said. In the city of Kerman, a farmworker named Prudencio Rivera said that ICE agents tracked him for two miles, said there was a deportation order for him that they did not present, broke his window when he refused to roll it down, physically pulled him from his car, threw him to the ground, and handcuffed him. After Rivera was brought to an immigration facility in Fresno, he showed officials there the same work authorization papers he showed to the abducting agents. He was eventually let go.

Strater described similar situations, which can result in cars being abandoned on the road with lights and ignition still on. She said that community members have assisted in returning vehicles to families, or obtained Ring camera footage that could shed light on ICE abductions.

There are no specific numbers of detainees who have been taken, and according to the UFW, ICE has been slow-walking reporting of detentions to create obstacles to legal representation. In one instance the UFW related, a man called his wife from a specific immigration detention facility, but the man’s name could not be found in a database of detainees. Without being present in the database, detainees cannot have access to attorneys, and Strater said that by the time they show up in the database, they have often been moved to other facilities.

The local mood is “tense,” Strater said. One incident last week featured an allegedly intoxicated off-duty ICE agent passing out on a local’s front yard, then assaulting the elderly resident and his daughter; the man then shot the agent in apparent self-defense. The agent was himself taken into custody for felony assault. Elsewhere, a car crash involving an ICE agent was reported.

Major local farm bureaus have been silent about the increased activity. Privately, UFW officials said that they have raised concerns but have been reluctant to speak out or put their names on any lawsuits.

The timing of the surge, a month before the elections, could be designed to chill voter mobilization and balloting from Hispanic residents. It also comes as some crops, like pomegranates, are being harvested. These are some of the last shifts farmworkers can get before the winter months. “We are entering into the time when farmworkers are dependent on every single hour,” Strater said. “They don’t have a choice but to show up for work.”

She added that farmworkers are changing their commuting patterns, like splitting up husbands and wives who work at the same facility to increase chances that someone will be available to pick up their children from day care.

As far as the effect on mobilization, streets in farmworker towns have been quiet the past couple of weeks, and some local festivals have been canceled. But advocates say it’s having the opposite effect, uniting opposition to Trump and building determination to remove his allies from office. The region has seen numerous protests from residents, student walkouts, and in one instance participation from Kerman Mayor Maria Pacheco, confronting ICE agents in a parking lot outside a Latino bakery. “You are not a resident of Kerman and you need to leave!” Pacheco told agents.

The UFW is continuing its registration and canvassing efforts, and officials believe the ICE raids will be top of mind for voters in the election. Asked about Valadao’s comments, Strater said, “He was elected to represent the people of the 22nd District, but he’s too much of a chickenshit to stand up to whoever is pulling the strings … He knows full well that these people are the backbone of the agricultural economy.”

In his statement last week, Valadao did say that “Hardworking farmworkers who are simply going to work, providing for their families, and contributing to our agricultural economy should not have to live in fear.” The UFW says his other comments contradict that alleged concern.

text:
U.S. Northern District of California Judge Trina Thompson joined three law professors to review major Supreme Court cases at a talk in September.

The panel discussed public trust in the judiciary and examined cases involving data privacy, criminal appeals, immigration enforcement and civil procedure.

Upcoming cases could affect gun rights, property seizures and the limits of government power.

Three law professors and a federal judge examined Supreme Court cases involving executive power, individual rights and immigration policy during a recent panel discussion at UC Law San Francisco.

Professors Rory Little, Richard Boswell and Scott Dodson joined U.S. Northern District of California Judge Trina Thompson for the law school’s 29th annual Supreme Court Review and Preview on Sept. 30.

Thompson discussed Louisiana v. Callais, on the role of race in drawing voting districts, and Olivier v. City of Brandon, in which the court unanimously ruled that a street preacher can sue over restrictions on where people can protest. She said the cases show how the court’s decisions shape political representation and individual rights, and that the justices can agree on major constitutional questions.

She also addressed Trump v. Barbara, where the court rejected the Trump administration’s effort to end birthright citizenship by executive order. The case raised questions about presidential authority and the meaning of the 14th Amendment’s Citizenship Clause.

“The decision illustrates how constitutional interpretation can place the judiciary directly in the middle of some of the most consequential disputes in American life,” Thompson said.

Little, who organized and moderated the panel, reviewed criminal cases from the court’s most recent term. In Chatrie v. United States, the court ruled that people have a reasonable expectation of privacy when it comes to cellphone location data held by companies such as Google. In Hunter v. United States, the court held that a defendant can sometimes appeal a conviction or sentence after agreeing to waive that right. The case raises questions about whether agreements are truly voluntary when people are under pressure, including in plea deals and consent to police searches.

Little said Hunter is “the most important criminal case of the term which no one’s heard of because it really puts things into doubt.”

Looking ahead, Little previewed two cases the court will hear this fall. One could decide if states and local governments can ban AR-15-style rifles. Another asks if Alaska’s seizure of an airplane used to haul a locally banned six-pack of beer is an excessive penalty under the Eighth Amendment.

Boswell, an immigrants’ rights expert, focused on cases involving the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including mass arrests and deportation, incarceration, elimination of prosecutorial discretion, firing of immigration judges and efforts to limit federal court review. He said immigrants challenging their detention have prevailed in the vast majority of nearly 80,000 habeas corpus cases brought in response to these policies, and that the caseload is placing enormous strains on courts and prosecutors.

“What [U.S. attorneys] are not doing when they’re in there on a habeas case … is they’re not dealing with serious crimes,” Boswell said. “They’re not dealing with drug trafficking and human trafficking.”

Dodson, director of UC Law SF’s Center for Litigation and Courts, analyzed rulings on civil procedure. He praised three unanimous decisions, including Berk v. Choy, which held that extra filing requirements for medical-malpractice claims in Delaware and other states don’t apply in federal court when they conflict with federal rules.

Dodson criticized other rulings, including Enbridge Energy, LP v. Nessel, which held that a 30-day deadline for removing a lawsuit from state to federal court cannot be extended through equitable tolling. Since the Court decided the issue under facts that would not justify equitable tolling anyway, he said it was unwise to use the case to reject equitable tolling for all cases. He argued that, in procedure cases, the Supreme Court should defer more to the views of procedure experts, such as professors, lower courts, and the federal rules advisory committees.

“The court should approach matters of federal civil procedure with a certain humility,” Dodson said.

Thompson emphasized the importance of public trust in the courts, especially as judges are increasingly viewed through a political lens. That trust, she said, cannot rest on whether people agree with every decision.

“The legitimacy of the judiciary does not come from being right in the eyes of everyone,” she said. “It comes from being faithful to the law, honest about the reasoning, open to scrutiny, and committed to treating every person who enters the courtroom with dignity.”
