text:
Federal immigration agents raided a housing construction site in Santa Fe on Tuesday morning and arrested several people, part of what builders said was a spate of visits to construction sites and other locations across the city for immigration enforcement.

“I spoke to a couple other builders. They’ve gone to quite a few construction sites in the city,” Vincent Pizzonia, founder and owner of Twilight Homes, said Tuesday.

His company is one of a few developers of the Los Brios site off of Agua Fría Street on the city’s immigrant-dense south side. A social media video captured a few men being walked off in handcuffs by agents marked with “ICE” and “ERO,” referring to Enforcement and Removal Operations.

Pizzonia said he was unsure if the video was of his contractors or those from another company at the housing development.

“It’s not just us,” he said, “all the building sites in Los Lunas, Rio Rancho, Albuquerque — and now Santa Fe.”

Officials from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to emails Tuesday seeking confirmation of the arrests in Santa Fe and further information about the people detained by the agency.

Arrests of immigrants have increased nationwide to historic levels in recent months, with the arrest totals released by the Department of Homeland Security in July and August reflecting all-time records. Data from September has not yet been disclosed.

‘Ghost town’ at big developments

The increase in immigration arrests and raids in some of New Mexico’s largest cities is taking a toll not only on construction workers and their families but on the homebuilding industry as it seeks to fill wide gaps in housing in the state, said New Mexico Homebuilders Association CEO Miles Conway.

Conway pointed to recent ICE raids at construction sites in Los Lunas and Albuquerque, part of what he said appears to be an uptick in immigration-related arrests in the region.

“This is going to be reflected not only in the lives of families that are residing in New Mexico, but it’s going to be reflected in our economy, because individuals are not coming to work, and the work of building housing in New Mexico is not moving forward,” he said.

“I’m hearing some of my builders saying that it’s just a ghost town out on these major building projects,” he continued. “Individuals that may absolutely have status — that may absolutely have paperwork to be in this country legally — are still feeling fear and reacting to what’s going on by not not going to work.”

The National Association of Home Builders has taken what has been called a rare and strong stance against the national surge in immigrant detention. The organization has also issued guidance to its members to inform them of their rights in situations where immigration agents show up at worksites — either for a raid or as part of an administrative audit, which includes advance notice.

Still, when a raid occurs, the situation can be “chaotic,” Conway noted, and subcontractors or employees could be at a site alone and unprepared to invoke their rights.

“I mean it’s such a human rights issue and a human dignity issue that we’re experiencing right now that it feels a little odd to be pointing towards our state’s economy, but you will see this reflected in the economic measurements of this summer in Santa Fe,” Conway said. “Just the people not going to work because they’re fearful of being displaced from their families.”

‘They’re in many places’

Following the Los Brios arrests around 9:30 a.m. Tuesday, Santa Fe Rapid Response, a team of civilian volunteers who respond to reports of ICE activity, had already dispatched teams around the city.

“It was a lot of activity today,” said member Sharon Argenbright. “More than I’ve ever seen. We kept getting messages and sightings.”

Argenbright was one of around eight responders who spent the morning warning local construction workers and nearby schools. She noted the group received a flurry of reports surpassing even the surge of arrests in August, which attorneys and advocates said ended with at least 15 people arrested over roughly a week.

At a separate construction site following the Los Brios arrests, she said volunteers found immigration authorities and pressured them out of the neighborhood before they could make any arrests.

“We noticed them, honked our horns and they drove away,” she said.

Gina Auz, president of the Latino Small Business Association, filmed the Los Brios arrests, with the video garnering more than 400,000 views on Facebook on Tuesday. In her video, she asks the men arrested to say their names “so we can tell your families.”

Following the video, Auz, who runs a local social media group popular for sharing Spanish-language news, filmed a livestream for her over 9,000 followers in which she urged construction and landscaping workers to stay home, joked they should start a new Netflix series instead of going to work and fielded questions from hundreds of concerned commenters.

“Gina, is it true they came to Las Palomas apartments?” one wrote.

“Are schools safe?” asked another.

“They’re in many places,” Auz said. “They’re in many places.”

text:
A Texas prosecutor said he was considering felony assault charges for an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who ran over a man following an attempted traffic stop and broke his leg in multiple places.

Sean Teare, district attorney for Harris county, said video of the incident in west Houston on Saturday morning, in which the officer’s unmarked SUV is seen veering into the man as he runs away across an empty parking lot, could support a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

A conviction carries a possible prison sentence of up to 20 years.

“It’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle,” Teare told NBC News, adding that his view was shared by “many other investigators” who had seen the footage.

The injured man, Miguel Parra-Hernandez, remained under ICE supervision at a hospital in Houston on Wednesday with serious hip and leg injuries that his representatives said would require a series of future surgeries.

ICE has conceded the 48-year-old was not the target of the traffic stop, but said he was in the country illegally.

The video showed the officer pursuing Parra-Hernandez in his vehicle in apparent contravention of new guidelines for traffic stops implemented this month after a series of violent and fatal confrontations involving federal immigration officers over the summer.

Teare is investigating the incident with the Harris county sheriff’s office, which said an ICE agent moved the pickup truck Parra-Hernandez and another unidentified person were riding in, then left the scene in the ICE vehicle before sheriff’s deputies arrived.

The district attorney told NBC that ICE was refusing to cooperate, and had denied his investigators’ request for access to information from the vehicle’s data recorder.

“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said.

“In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that. [You] put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”

He said he believed two other persons from “an entirely different operation” were in custody in the back of the ICE vehicle when the driver began to pursue Parra-Hernandez, and that his office was working to ensure they remained in the country to provide evidence as material witnesses.

“I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the US that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” Teare said.

“Every single person out there [was] in danger again.”

His team, he added, had gathered evidence that “goes above” the surveillance video aired by multiple local media outlets, and set up a portal for videos or photographs of the incident that does not require witnesses to provide citizenship or immigration information.

ICE did not respond to a request from the Guardian for comment. Over the weekend, an agency spokesperson said the target of the early-morning operation was another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, an undocumented immigrant with multiple prior arrests and a final order of removal signed by a judge.

At a press conference on Monday, Kim Bruno, Parra-Hernandez’s lawyer, and Cesar Espinosa, executive director of the immigrant advocacy group Fiel Houston, told reporters that he had never met Mendoza-Cervantes.

Bruno said her client fled because he did not know who was in the dark-colored vehicle that was not using lights or a siren. He has no criminal record, and was on his way to work when ICE agents appeared, she said.

NBC cited an ICE spokesperson who said allegations Parra-Hernandez was intentionally struck were “reckless and false” and “disgusting smears … peddled by the media”.

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” the spokesperson said.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is fast-tracking a $100 million domestic surveillance program to put 142 intelligence agents in more than two dozen cities and the District of Columbia, in what contracting and surveillance experts said would be a significant expansion of the agency’s ability to reach into private lives.

The new program is called the Enforcement and Removal Operations Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, or ERO ONE, described in documents posted last month on federal procurement websites.

More from Whitney Curry Wimbish

Under the program, agents would analyze classified and unclassified information to identify “trends, patterns, relationships, threats, and intelligence gaps,” and provide ICE with briefings for Enforcement and Removal Operation missions, according to a statement of work published on September 18. A forecasting document published a week earlier said that the solicitation will likely be released on December 10. Intelligence contracting experts said the timeline suggests ICE will award the contract around February.

“It looks dangerously like the construction of an internal spying agency,” said Jay Stanley, senior policy analyst with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, who has written extensively on immigration agencies’ mass surveillance. “It’s a nightmare in the making.”

It’s also a weapon that the government will likely use against not only undocumented immigrants, but everyone else, too. That includes political enemies, intelligence experts said. Speaking with the Prospect on Monday as news broke that the Trump regime had raided progressive Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home, former military intelligence analyst Michael Wriston said that “you’d expect to see more of this” under ERO ONE.

“Not just necessarily sitting members of Congress, but anyone, and especially members of the immigrant community,” Wriston said. “No one is safe. No one.”

THE PLAN DOES NOT SPECIFY WHAT OR WHOM ICE is looking for with this increased spying capability. But one of the components that caused former intelligence contractors’ concern was that ERO ONE agents will analyze both classified and nonclassified information to produce “network, link and relationship” analyses. That type of analysis involves researching not only a target, but also every other person to whom they’re connected, including household members, family members, friends, acquaintances, or the person with whom they carpool to work.

According to the statement of work, contractors will be tasked with conducting analytical research “to identify and assess relationships among individuals, organizations, locations, events, activities, data points, and other entities.” They will review information to identify “known, reported, or potential relationships; recurring patterns; organizational structures; associations; areas of convergence; temporal or geographic connections; and other linkages relevant to the assigned intelligence requirement.” Contractors will then “evaluate the significance and reliability” of the relationships and “prepare link charts, network diagrams, timelines, analytical summaries, written assessments, or other related products” for ICE to use.

Military intelligence agents compile the same type of research, Wriston said. He knows because he did that job.

“We’ve seen this time and time again. It’s the imperial boomerang,” said Wriston, who is also a data journalist and the founder of ICE watchdog group Project Salt Box, where he reported on ERO ONE the day the first document went live and has written about it since. “These are the kinds of things that happened in Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, for years. Now that methodology is being brought into the ICE space.”

Federal documents likewise do not detail the specific sources of information agents will analyze, only that all agents must possess previously awarded active top secret clearance, with eligibility to access Sensitive Compartmented Information. That’s a type of information that must be accessed through certain formal control systems managed by the Director of National Intelligence, a position held by Trump ally Jay Clayton. The agents will not make any decisions about what to do with the information they compile.

Wriston said that except for the fact that ICE officials are trying to make immigration a matter of national security, it’s unclear why they need this program when they already have the Homeland Security Investigations unit, which conducted the raid on Omar’s house, to research targets. His immediate worry, he said, is that the program will make it easier for the government to find terrified immigrants hiding at home because they think they’ll be safe there.

ICE PLANS TO SEND THE 142 AGENTS, plus two project managers, to locations in Atlanta, Boston, Buffalo, Chicago, Dallas, D.C., Denver, Detroit, El Paso, Harlingen (Texas), Houston, Laguna Niguel (California), Los Angeles, Miami, New Orleans, New York, Newark, Philadelphia, Phoenix, Salt Lake City, San Antonio, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, St. Paul, and Williston (Vermont), according to the statement of work.

Details in the document, and the rapid timeline, show that the Trump administration intends to use the program immediately, said Brian Murphy, a government contractor who worked for 25 years with ICE parent agency DHS. It’s rare for the government to only want workers with top secret clearance, he said.

“I’ve only seen it when there is an imminent need to work on something right now,” he told the Prospect. “Trump has two years in office. He can’t wait … they want to get rolling on this immediately.”

The program description is so broad that Murphy said he thinks the goal goes beyond targeting immigrants. “I think it’s darker than that,” because the agency could use the intelligence to attack people with identities and views the Trump regime doesn’t like. “The question for DHS is, what is the threat they’re trying to go after?”

The federal government can easily change who qualifies as a threat and produce data that backs up the reasoning, Murphy said, and used as an example annual Homeland Threat Assessments. In 2020, Secretary of Homeland Security Chad Wolf identified white supremacist extremists as “the most persistent and lethal threat in the Homeland.” But by last year, that threat had disappeared from the report, except to appear once in a glossary of terms. The rest of the report focused heavily on Trump administration priorities as national security threats, including immigrants crossing the border with Mexico and transnational criminal organizations.

In addition, the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti have shown how the government views protesters against ICE abductions as an abiding threat. In a national security directive known as NSPM-7, President Trump identified anti-fascist protesters as domestic terrorists and proposed an architecture to disrupt and counter dissent.

“If you want to draw a narrative that the real threat to America is whatever you want it to be, you can very easily do that. You just stop gathering intel on militias,” Murphy said. “It’s like any other police state. If you ask it to find something to make my opponents the enemy, well, you can do that.”

Legal liability should be a major concern for anyone who bids on the ERO ONE contract, Murphy said, because it’s unclear whether the information they’d be charged with accessing had been gathered legally. He added, “It’s very, very concerning that they’re fast-tracking this.”

Stanley, the ACLU analyst, noted that immigration officials across agencies have been using an excessive amount of surveillance tools for years, including their “Stingray” cell tower simulators, automatic license plate readers, and tools that track location from cellphones. They use a facial recognition and biometric collection app called Mobile Fortify, a Palantir app called ImmigrationOS to track immigrants’ movements, and buy data from LexisNexis to identify someone’s family and work history. ERO ONE would draw on all of that information, plus an expanded group of sources to reach into the private lives of anyone it wants, intelligence experts said.

ICE already knows its potential bidders for ERO ONE, said Diana Brozi, the procurement specialist listed on the document. She told the Prospect it was unlikely the agency would hold an industry day and declined to provide further information.

DHS did not respond to a request for information or comment on the claim that the program could be used to spy on political enemies.

authors: Diego Medel, San Antonio Report, www.houstonpublicmedia.org
description:
San Antonio filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday seeking to halt development of a planned immigration detention facility on the East Side until federal authorities comply with environmental review requirements.
The city is asking a federal judge to prevent DHS and ICE from moving forward with development until the required environmental review is completed.
Since February, city officials have sent five letters to DHS and ICE seeking details about the proposed facility, including environmental reviews, permitting requirements and opportunities for public input.

Those concerns have already prompted additional scrutiny from City Council.
text:
This story first appeared in the San Antonio Report.

San Antonio filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday seeking to halt development of a planned immigration detention facility on the East Side until federal authorities comply with environmental review requirements.

The lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement seeks to stop the conversion of a nearly 640,000-square-foot warehouse acquired by ICE in January on Southeast Loop 410 into an immigration detention and processing facility capable of holding up to 1,500 people.

City Attorney Andy Segovia announced the legal action Tuesday morning alongside Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones and several City Council members, marking the city’s most significant effort yet to challenge the proposed facility.

The lawsuit centers on the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, which requires federal agencies to assess the potential environmental effects of major projects before proceeding. The city is asking a federal judge to prevent DHS and ICE from moving forward with development until the required environmental review is completed.

Segovia said those reviews go beyond assessing air and water quality to consider how a project could affect the surrounding community, including its economy, history and culture.

“With a facility of this size and scope, within the core urban core of San Antonio, these sorts of reviews are even more critical,” Segovia said. “It’s very clear to see that there will be these impacts, and the law is there to make sure that those impacts are mitigated.”

The lawsuit follows months of unsuccessful attempts by city officials to obtain information about the conversion, development plans and potential environmental impacts of the facility.

Since February, city officials have sent five letters to DHS and ICE seeking details about the proposed facility, including environmental reviews, permitting requirements and opportunities for public input.

Federal officials responded to one letter in June, promising to coordinate with the city, seek community feedback and share engineering and design reports before beginning work.

But Jones said the city has received none of that information, even as ICE awarded a $17.3 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services, a contractor involved in Florida’s controversial “Alligator Alcatraz” detention facility, to renovate the warehouse.

“We have been very patient with the federal authorities, in particular DHS and ICE, on this issue,” Jones said. “San Antonio is done waiting.”

What could the lawsuit accomplish?

While the lawsuit may not permanently stop ICE from opening the facility, city leaders hope the environmental review process will create enough obstacles for federal authorities to reconsider the project altogether.

“So while the legal action is to delay, our hope is that looking at the significant impact that facility may have, that the department makes their independent decision based on that information they obtain to do something different,” Segovia said.

Segovia said he expects the preliminary environmental assessment of the warehouse’s conversion to find significant impacts, potentially triggering a more extensive environmental impact study that could take months to complete.

District 2 Councilman Jalen McKee-Rodriguez, who represents the district where the proposed facility is located, pointed to other cities where concerns raised by local governments have prompted federal authorities to reconsider or cancel plans for immigration detention centers altogether.

“It has become clear, DHS has no intention of doing its due diligence,” McKee-Rodriguez said.

He said a review of the proposed facility would likely identify problems with its proximity to schools, parks and community centers, as well as the infrastructure needed to accommodate up to 1,500 people.

Those concerns have already prompted additional scrutiny from City Council.

Last week, council members directed city departments and local utilities to conduct independent assessments of how the facility could affect water, wastewater, electricity and emergency services in the surrounding area.

The studies could provide additional information to support the city’s legal challenge. Similar concerns about local water and power capacity have reportedly led ICE to abandon plans to convert two warehouses into processing facilities in Pennsylvania.

While most City Council members have supported the legal challenge, council members Marc Whyte (D10) and Misty Spears (D9) have criticized it as an expensive effort that will do little more than delay the facility.

“This is political theater, nothing more than political theater that, unfortunately, my colleagues and the mayor want to engage in,” Whyte said in an interview following the announcement.

Whyte disputed the likelihood that the lawsuit would lead ICE to abandon the facility, arguing that similar legal challenges elsewhere have merely delayed federal projects.

“That is what I anticipate is going to happen here. Sure, the federal government could decide that they don’t want to be in San Antonio,” Whyte said. “But it’s not going to be because of this lawsuit.”

Spears questioned why the city was raising environmental concerns about the ICE facility when it had not raised similar objections to the city’s former Migrant Resource Center.

“The double standard is glaring,” Spears said. “Suing the federal government for enforcing our nation’s immigration laws is political theater at taxpayers’ expense.”

Whyte estimated the lawsuit could cost the city $500,000 or more, arguing that money would be better spent on public safety and infrastructure.

Segovia declined to provide an estimated cost for the suit Tuesday, saying the city had shared preliminary figures with council members but that the final expense would depend on the federal government’s response and how far the litigation proceeds.

Jones defended the decision to pursue legal action despite the potential cost, arguing that the community deserves answers about the facility and its possible long-term economic effects.

“To the point of wasted money, you tell me what is the price tag for respect?” she said. “You’ve got to respect this community. Our community deserves to understand what is happening at that facility.”

DHS and ICE did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

title: These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead. - ProPublica
authors: Melissa Sanchez, Anna Clark, Antoine Maillard
description:
Advocates across the country say they’re seeing signs of an alarming increase in the numbers of domestic violence victims who are detained and deported.
The arrest and detention of domestic violence victims is, in part, an unanticipated consequence of an effort meant to keep them safe.
There’s no comprehensive way to track how often this happens or how many domestic violence victims have been detained by ICE or deported.
“There’s been a chilling impact to women coming forward in domestic violence situations due to what’s going on,” Becker said.
Some were deported, including at least two Mexican women who were also arrested in Kent County on suspicion of domestic violence.
text:
They were victims, not abusers. That’s what they told police officers, attorneys, visitors and anyone else who would listen. It didn’t matter. The women were all taken to a sprawling immigration detention center in the woods of west Michigan and handed thin jumpsuits — red, to mark them as a high security risk.

Inside the North Lake Processing Center, they talked about the men whose calls to police landed them there. The boyfriends or husbands who threatened to get them deported and cut them off from their children. The men, or sometimes women, who hit them, pulled their hair or choked them, bruising their throats.

They didn’t know where to go for help before, but now, in the confines of a cold cellblock in a former prison, the women helped one another. If one spoke to somebody on the outside who could connect them with advice, legal aid or money for the commissary, she’d pass around a tablet used for calls so others could tell their stories.

Migladys Bermudez, an immigration attorney in southeast Michigan, remembers a call in May from a Peruvian woman detained at North Lake. Her name was Pilar, and she’d heard about Bermudez from a fellow detainee who had been a client. Pilar told Bermudez about the boyfriend she tried to escape before her arrest, when she used makeup to cover the marks she said he left on her face. But he had accused her of being the abuser, resulting in her arrest.

Pilar handed the tablet to a Cuban woman named Leya. Over the echoes of the other detainees’ chatter, she described how her boyfriend insulted her, isolated her and gave her a black eye. Then, after grabbing him by the arm during an argument, she was the one behind bars, separated from their nursing daughter. On video calls, the girl didn’t seem to recognize her mother anymore. She stopped calling her “Mamá.”

Bermudez was taken aback. All three women in that chain — the former client, Pilar and Leya — said they were trying to get out of abusive relationships when they were arrested by local police on domestic violence allegations. In all three cases, the charges were dropped or never filed at all. The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained the first woman during a routine check-in a few months after her charges were dropped. The others were handed over to ICE by local officials.

It’s long been intimidating for immigrants who suffered abuse to call 911, regardless of who was in the White House. They knew — and their abusers knew — that their immigration status made them vulnerable. But previous administrations treated victims as just that, people who needed help, not as targets for deportation. Bipartisan coalitions in Congress have long supported the Violence Against Women Act, which creates a pathway toward legal status for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence or other serious crimes.

Now, under President Donald Trump, all bets are off. On inauguration day, his administration rescinded guidelines that largely prevented immigration agents from making arrests at sensitive locations — including domestic violence shelters and hospitals. About a week later, the administration eliminated key protections granted to VAWA applicants and other crime victims. For the first time in decades, immigration authorities could disregard those protections and more freely arrest, detain and deport immigrant victims.

Life became more harrowing in other ways for immigrants who were victims of domestic violence. Federal immigration agents made arrests outside specialized domestic violence courts. And the administration persuaded more and more local police and jails to carry out the president’s mass deportation campaign, sweeping still more immigrants into custody.

Even communities without these so-called 287(g) agreements are helping the government round people up. In west Michigan’s Kent County, where Pilar and Leya were arrested, the county jail turned over more immigrants to ICE in the first six months of 2026 than it did during the entire Biden administration.

Advocates across the country say they’re seeing signs of an alarming increase in the numbers of domestic violence victims who are detained and deported. And many immigrants are staying in abusive relationships, fearful of calling for help or even stepping outside their homes.

“It’s just probably the most dangerous time for immigrant women right now who are victims of domestic violence,” said Bermudez, who took on Leya’s immigration case.

The arrest and detention of domestic violence victims is, in part, an unanticipated consequence of an effort meant to keep them safe. In much of the country, law enforcement officers are encouraged — or even required — to make an arrest when they have probable cause to believe that a domestic violence assault has taken place. Sometimes victims are mistaken as the abuser and taken into custody. Then, if they’re immigrants, they can be turned over to ICE — even if they were never criminally charged.

There’s no comprehensive way to track how often this happens or how many domestic violence victims have been detained by ICE or deported. But ProPublica spoke with a half-dozen alleged victims who were locked up together in a single facility, North Lake, and reviewed police records about others who were there, too. Their stories offer a picture of why Congress created programs like VAWA in the first place, and what’s at stake when those guardrails are taken away.

A coalition of immigrant survivors and advocates have sued the Trump administration, saying changes to how immigrant victims are treated not only undermined public safety, but also broke promises enshrined in federal law and policy.

“We were seeing our clients be more scared, be systematically targeted, be arrested, and deported very quickly,” said Kathleen Rivas, supervising attorney of the survivors team at Public Counsel, a law firm that’s involved in the litigation.

In May, a federal judge ordered the government to restore protections while the case played out. The Trump administration has appealed the order.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.”

But Leya, Pilar and other immigrants we interviewed have no criminal records. And advocates said communities are less safe now because immigrants are afraid to call police when their partners hurt them. This gives more ammunition to the threats of their abusers, said Casey Carter Swegman, director of public policy at the Tahirih Justice Center, a national nonprofit that advocates for immigrant survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault and human trafficking.

“Certainly more immigrant survivors are feeling like the violence and abuse they experience behind the closed door is somehow more tolerable than the violence and abuse they could experience if they tried to leave,” she said.

The first time her boyfriend’s fist slammed into her face was in July 2025, Leya recalled. They were living in Florida with his relatives. Only a month before, Leya gave birth to their daughter.

One night, she said, he heard her laugh in the kitchen with his mother and a man his mother was dating. Leya’s boyfriend flew into a jealous rage, she said, and punched her a few feet from their sleeping baby.

Leya called 911 but hung up when the operator answered. She was afraid of what might happen. She was 26; her boyfriend was a decade her senior. Leya, a recent immigrant from Cuba, had applied for status and was in active immigration proceedings. She said he was a permanent resident, with permission to work in the U.S. and better command of English. She felt trapped.

Sheriff’s deputies arrived and spoke with Leya and her boyfriend. They took photos of her puffy and bruised face, with the white of her left eye bright red. Her boyfriend said the injury occurred during an “argument,” according to the report, but he didn’t specify how. He was arrested on suspicion of domestic battery.

Leya said her boyfriend’s mother threw her out that night. Unsure of where to go, she and her daughter moved in with another one of his relatives. Pursuing a criminal case felt daunting. She said his relatives urged her to drop the charges and reconcile with him. Eventually, she asked prosecutors to drop the charge because the battery took place in “a moment of impulse that he feels very sorry for,” records show. Her boyfriend didn’t enter a plea before the case was dismissed.

Like other immigrants interviewed for this story, Leya asked not to be fully identified because of her pending immigration case, and because she worries about repercussions for her and her daughter.

She and Pilar also asked that ProPublica not interview their alleged abusers because they’re afraid the men will interfere with their cases, hurt them or take away their children. To report their stories and get their partners’ perspective, we reviewed records from law enforcement, immigration court proceedings and habeas corpus petitions seeking their release from detention. We also interviewed attorneys, family and others who interacted with them.

Soon after the Florida arrest, Leya and her boyfriend moved to the city of Wyoming, Michigan, a suburb of Grand Rapids that’s a magnet for immigrants who come for jobs in manufacturing and food processing. The unpretentious city is dotted with temporary staffing agencies, money-wiring businesses and Mexican restaurants.

Leya said their relationship worsened. Her boyfriend pushed her, pulled her hair and broke her phone, she said. He made her delete her social media accounts and isolated her from friends and family. They fought about money and talked about breaking up. One night in April, during an argument, he called the police.

“I’m having problems with my wife,” he said in Spanish, according to a recording of the call. The operator asked if there had been any violence. “No, no, no. None,” he said. “Just a discussion.”

He told officers who came to their apartment complex that Leya got angry because he had talked to an ex-girlfriend, according to body camera footage and a police report. When he tried to leave, he said, Leya pushed him and grabbed his arm. Then she attempted to hang up his phone when he dialed 911.

He said he wasn’t injured, though he accused her of hitting him several times a few days earlier.

Officers interviewed his brother, who mentioned the arrest in Florida, according to bodycam footage. “They had a cycle of problems where she called the police for abuse and he was detained for three days,” he said in Spanish. “My brother is trying to avoid having that happen again.”

The police report doesn’t mention the earlier arrest.

Footage of the interview with Leya was redacted due to state privacy laws, in part because she was interviewed inside their residence, unlike her boyfriend, who was interviewed outside. According to the police report, she “minimized” the argument and said there was no physical contact. She acknowledged trying to hang up the phone.

In an interview with ProPublica, Leya said they argued when she learned he sent money to his ex-girlfriend, who is the mother of his son. At the same time, she said, he had told her he couldn’t afford to buy diapers for their daughter. She said she has never hit him.

Officers arrested Leya on suspicion of domestic assault and interfering with a 911 call. They didn’t arrest her boyfriend or seek charges against him. Leya said she didn’t tell officers she was a victim of abuse because she thought she’d be able to tell a judge.

She never got a chance.

The Wyoming Police Department’s written policy encourages officers to make an arrest in incidents involving domestic violence “when there is reasonable cause to believe an assault was committed.”

Arrests demonstrate that “violence in the home is recognized as a serious crime,” according to Michigan’s law enforcement training manual on domestic violence. This approach is common across the country. Twenty-four states require an arrest when there’s probable cause of a domestic assault.

But domestic violence scenes can be chaotic, with both partners accusing each other of being the aggressor. It can be difficult for officers to understand what happened, said Erin Ross, a former domestic violence prosecutor who works at the national nonprofit Vera Institute of Justice. Sometimes, the wrong person ends up in handcuffs.

“The complexity of DV situations can thus lead to survivors being criminalized by the very system meant to protect them,” Ross and her co-authors wrote in a 2025 report about the effects of arrests on domestic violence survivors.

The Vera report doesn’t touch on immigration. But Ross and a dozen other domestic violence advocates across the country told ProPublica that immigrants who don’t speak English or understand their rights are, under the Trump administration, especially vulnerable to an arrest that can have irreversible consequences.

ProPublica reviewed hundreds of habeas corpus petitions filed nationwide since January 2025, in which immigrants challenged their ICE detention on constitutional grounds. We found dozens of petitioners who were arrested on suspicion of domestic violence and turned over to ICE, even though they were never charged or their charges were dropped. Using jail and police records from Florida and Michigan, as well as news reports, we identified even more cases.

In their petitions, several immigrants said that officers mistook them for the aggressor. The underlying arrest records show that officers often had to make close calls in messy cases where it was unclear who was the victim and who was the aggressor. Either way, under Trump, there’s little grace for immigrants.

In one case in Florida, a state where sheriff’s offices cooperate with immigration authorities, a deputy came upon a Venezuelan couple arguing in the street in November 2025. In his report, the deputy said the woman pulled at her husband’s pants, necklace and arm, leaving marks on his body. The woman said her husband had taken her keys and phone. She didn’t want to be left stranded, she said, so she ran after him.

She was charged with misdemeanor battery; her husband wasn’t charged. The woman was turned over to ICE while the case was pending. Prosecutors later dropped charges. The sheriff’s report didn’t mention any allegations of prior domestic violence, but the woman later said that, during their marriage, her husband had beaten her and threatened to kill her. In her habeas corpus petition, she said she was “afraid to report the abuse to the police.”

The woman was released in May, but during the five months she was incarcerated, her husband took their daughters out of state, her attorney told ProPublica. She still hasn’t seen the girls in person.

For Leya, it was a shock to find herself handcuffed, sitting in the back of a police cruiser, headed toward the Kent County jail. She was silent during the 15-minute ride, unable to make sense of what had just happened: “I had suffered from domestic violence,” she said. “But the one who ended up in trouble was me.”

The next day, a detective asked the prosecutor’s office to file charges against her. Prosecutors declined to do so, saying there was insufficient evidence, there were no injuries and Leya hadn’t successfully interfered with the phone call.

Still, she wasn’t released.

Leya had no criminal history, apart from this arrest, according to a DHS record. But her fingerprints had been run against state and federal databases, flagging ICE officials who could match them with her prints from when she arrived in the U.S. In addition, Leya said, a jail official asked about her status, and she told him she was waiting for an immigration court hearing.

ICE issued a detainer, essentially asking the jail to hold Leya until agents could pick her up. Kent County officials honored their request. A day later, Leya was at the detention center in the woods.

She cried in despair over her daughter. They’d never been separated. The 80 miles between Wyoming and North Lake seemed infinite. Her breasts ached from the drying milk. Leya wondered whether she’d be deported and if their separation would be permanent.

From a narrow window in her cell, she saw people outside holding signs, protesting ICE. She could hear their chants in English. Though she had trouble understanding them, she felt comforted by the care of strangers.

Inside, she familiarized herself with the routines. She spent most of her time in a large, open room with other women in red. Cameras eyed them as they talked about their children and upcoming court dates. They shared contact information for relatives in their home countries in case one of them got deported and had nowhere to go. To pass the hours, they watched telenovelas, played rounds of Uno and pieced together jigsaw puzzles of forests and farms.

Leya grew close to a few women from Latin America and Eastern Europe who said they, too, had been in abusive relationships. Several had called police for help, records show. A Honduran woman said her partner tried to choke her. A Dominican woman said her husband, a U.S. citizen, hit her, pulled her hair and chased her with a stick.

Then there was Pilar, Leya’s first cellmate. The asylum seeker from Peru had also been arrested on suspicion of domestic violence in the city of Wyoming.

Pilar, her boyfriend and her teenage daughter called 911 five times in the 15 months before her arrest, records show. On one occasion, Pilar’s daughter said she worried that the boyfriend would hurt her mom; according to bodycam footage, Pilar assured officers that everything was fine. On another, the man said he experienced mental abuse and wanted to find a shelter. On yet another, Pilar said she just wanted him to leave.

None of these calls ended in an arrest. Officers ensured that the boyfriend had another place to stay when he sought help, and they told Pilar to call back if he tried to return and hurt her, according to the footage. They advised the couple to go to civil court for future disputes over money and property.

In an interview with ProPublica from North Lake, Pilar, 48, said that her boyfriend took financial advantage of her and physically assaulted her. And in her habeas corpus petition, she described the relationship as one of “physical, mental, psychological, economic abuse.” Her sister took a photo of the bruises around Pilar’s neck and feared the worst. “I would tell her to leave that man,” she said.

Pilar said she was ashamed to go to her job at a food-processing plant with bruises on her face. She wondered what her co-workers would think. She distanced herself from relatives and friends. Pilar said she never told the police the full story because she worried about the possible repercussions — not for herself, but for her boyfriend. She didn’t want him to be deported. Despite everything, she loved him and felt he loved her.

One night in October 2025, her boyfriend drove up to their apartment complex in a rental car. The couple argued in the parking lot. He called 911.

“I need police,” he said over and over in English.

Pilar called moments later: “This man is leaving my house and he’s not giving me my keys,” she screamed in Spanish. “This man has hurt me. He has scratched my whole arm.”

When officers arrived, they separated the couple. The boyfriend said that Pilar slapped his head, grabbed his shirt and tried to pull him out of the car while he was in the driver’s seat, according to bodycam footage and the police report. One side of his T-shirt was torn. He said he never assaulted Pilar and any injuries were her own fault. “I’ve never hit her,” he said in Spanish.

He told officers that he’d become a U.S. permanent resident two months earlier and that Pilar was jealous. “She is making this up because she knows she can get papers,” he said.

Pilar insisted she was the victim. She showed officers the scratch marks on her arm and said her boyfriend was to blame. She begged them to make him return the apartment keys, according to bodycam footage and a police report. “I’ve been trying to kick him out for a while and he won’t leave, and he doesn’t want to help pay the rent,” she said in Spanish.

An officer asked how her boyfriend’s shirt got ripped. Pilar said she grabbed onto him when he started driving away in order to avoid being dragged by the car. The officer asked her several more times about the ripped shirt. Pilar told him she wanted to speak to a lawyer.

In their report, police noted that the boyfriend had called 911 first. His shirt was ripped. Pilar’s wasn’t. If the boyfriend had thrown her down, the officer wrote, then her shirt should have been ripped because he was “much taller and heavier (around 80lbs more).”

Her boyfriend wasn’t arrested. Pilar was.

Wyoming Public Safety Chief Kip Snyder declined to speak about the arrests of Pilar or Leya. In an email to ProPublica, he said officers don’t “participate in enforcing federal immigration laws. We encourage trust and cooperation with all residents and aim to ensure that everyone feels safe reporting crimes or seeking assistance.”

Shortly after Pilar’s arrest, a police detective asked the prosecutor’s office to file domestic violence charges against both her and her boyfriend.

Prosecutors declined to file any charges, citing insufficient evidence. Pilar wasn’t released. Apart from this arrest, she had no criminal history, according to DHS records. She also had a pending asylum case.

Still, ICE put a detainer on her and jail officials turned her over.

A few years earlier, Kent County Sheriff Michelle Lajoye-Young said a handoff like this wouldn’t happen.

In 2019, she announced that deputies would stop automatically honoring detainers and instead require warrants signed by a federal judge or magistrate. The move came after a U.S. citizen — a Marine combat veteran — was transferred from her jail into ICE custody.

“There needed to be a judicial oversight inserted into that process to give us the assurance that somebody wasn’t erroneously detained without due process,” Lajoye-Young said around that time.

Trump called Kent a “sanctuary jurisdiction.” The label haunted the county, which in the 2016 election voted for Trump. A national think tank that aims to reduce immigration put Kent County on its list of sanctuary communities, while Republican state lawmakers tried to compel its cooperation with federal authorities.

Yet it’s unclear whether Lajoye-Young ever delivered on her promise. ProPublica requested copies of all department policies, procedures, memos and instructions on how it handles ICE detainers since 2018. None said a judicial warrant was needed. ProPublica also asked for copies of judicial warrants for Pilar and Leya. The county said no such records exist.

Lajoye-Young, who retired last week, declined interview requests. Sgt. Scott Dietrich, a spokesperson for the sheriff’s office, didn’t directly answer questions about whether the policy was ever implemented. But in a statement he said that detainers are “handled under applicable law and established policy, consistent with our commitment to public safety, due process, and fair and impartial enforcement.”

Gema Lowe, an organizer with the local chapter of an immigrant rights group, said the sheriff had backtracked on her promise and wasn’t being forthright. “I don’t understand why they’re being secretive,” she said.

The shift deepened the mistrust among immigrants in a county with one of the state’s fastest-growing immigrant populations. Lowe, an immigrant herself from Mexico, said she advises victims to think twice before reporting domestic violence to the police because of the risk of arrest and deportation, while pointing them to other local resources like shelters.

She and others said the stakes are especially high now. ICE arrests have skyrocketed under Trump. Nobody is off limits, including immigrants with pending asylum claims and no criminal records.

And more local authorities are helping ICE make arrests. In January 2025, fewer than 150 state and local law enforcement agencies had signed 287(g) agreements with DHS to help carry out the president’s deportation agenda. That number has ballooned to more than 2,600 today.

“Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country,” a DHS spokesperson said. “We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement works together with us.”

Kent County doesn’t have a 287(g) agreement. Still, the jail hands over the vast majority of people with detainers to ICE, records show. Dozens of people who were turned over to ICE this year had their criminal charges dropped, or, like Pilar and Leya, were never charged in the first place.

Dietrich said the dismissal of a criminal charge “does not, by itself, mean the original arrest lacked probable cause.” The sheriff’s office also doesn’t “determine whether criminal charges are ultimately prosecuted, nor does it determine whether an individual is deported,” he said.

DHS told ProPublica in a statement that both Leya and Pilar “illegally entered the country” in 2022 and that both “will receive due process” in their immigration proceedings.

Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker said he hadn’t heard of victims getting detained by ICE after calling the police. In his experience, he said, more perpetrators with active cases get deported.

Becker said he tries to get the message out that his team serves all victims, regardless of their immigration status. He’s aware that immigrants are reluctant to seek help. His own staff has told him that victims are afraid to testify or file restraining orders. They don’t want their partners — often the breadwinners and the fathers of their children — to be deported.

“There’s been a chilling impact to women coming forward in domestic violence situations due to what’s going on,” Becker said.

As the months passed at North Lake, Leya watched as women she befriended started to leave.

Some were deported, including at least two Mexican women who were also arrested in Kent County on suspicion of domestic violence. Others were released. New women took their cells. Some told Leya that they, too, had been arrested after 911 calls about domestic violence.

Leya fought for her freedom. She met with volunteers from Kent County, who raised money to hire her lawyers and pay for a required physical exam and fees. Even her ex-boyfriend, the one who she said gave her a black eye, wrote a letter on her behalf to help her case, calling her “a calm person.” He explained that he had called the police after their argument “escalated” and that “problems are situations that can happen in any relationship.”

Leya, he added, “deserves a second opportunity to remain in this country and be close to our daughter, as our baby truly needs her very much.” While Leya was locked up, their little girl celebrated her first birthday, got her first teeth and took her first steps.

At virtual hearings, Leya sat with her arms crossed, her dark, wavy hair neatly braided in cornrows and wearing an oversized coat over her red uniform. She tried to follow the discussion of people who seemed to have her life in their hands.

In late August, a judge granted Leya bond. While her immigration case played out, she could be free.

It was a profound relief. At the same time, it felt awful to leave behind her friends. It seemed like some of them were never getting out. Pilar was approaching a year in detention.

Four months after her arrest, Leya walked out of the old prison. She thought about how she would live on her own now and support her daughter.

She promised herself she wouldn’t go back to the man who hurt her.

title: New Democratic Bill Would Abolish ICE and Shut Down DHS - Newsweek
description:
"There are legitimate reasons to reconsider how DHS operates," Adam Klein, a former senior DHS official and co-founderof Globali.ai, told Newsweek.
"Immigration enforcement, detention practices, civil liberties, accountability, and the department's increasingly aggressive law enforcement posture all deserve serious scrutiny.
Eliminating or relocating agencies does not eliminate the government's responsibilities for border security, immigration enforcement, disaster response, cybersecurity, or counterterrorism," Klein said.
"America’s brave ICE agents put their lives on the line every day to enforce U.S. law and arrest criminal illegal aliens—including gang members, rapists, and murderers.
Representative Ramirez should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district—NOT vilifying law enforcement," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek Tuesday.
text:
A House Democrat has introduced legislation that would abolish the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and replace it with a new department focused on community safety, three weeks before an election where immigration policy is likely to have an influence on voters.

The "Reimagining Safety Act," introduced by Illinois Representative Delia Ramirez Tuesday, goes beyond previous plans to simply abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) by dismantling the parent department set up in the wake of 9/11.

The Congresswoman's spokesperson told Newsweek that the bill would keep vital functions such as FEMA and the TSA going under different departments, with a separate civil immigration system under the Department of Justice.

Read More on Politics

Ramirez has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration policies, which have also seen widespread pushback from Democrats across the U.S., but the sweeping nature of the proposal is likely to draw scrutiny so close to the midterms.

"There are legitimate reasons to reconsider how DHS operates," Adam Klein, a former senior DHS official and co-founderof Globali.ai, told Newsweek. "Immigration enforcement, detention practices, civil liberties, accountability, and the department's increasingly aggressive law enforcement posture all deserve serious scrutiny.

"Congresswoman Ramirez's proposal raises important questions about whether the department has moved too far from its original mission. My concern is the distance between what the legislation proposes and the operational responsibilities that still need to be performed. Eliminating or relocating agencies does not eliminate the government's responsibilities for border security, immigration enforcement, disaster response, cybersecurity, or counterterrorism," Klein said.

What the Bill Would Do

"Instead of the weapon DHS has proven to be, we need a department built on the best parts of who we are and can be, and the best examples of how we can take care of each other in hard times. I am proud to have led that work with the organizations in my district and nationally," Ramirez said in a press release.

"Building something new, creating in a time of destruction, is a revolutionary act. It is proof of our hope and belief in what is possible even in dark times. A different world is possible because the people have the power to reshape our government and reimagine how we cultivate safety and collective well-being."

The overarching plan outlined in the bill is to dismantle DHS after 25 years. ICE would be scrapped altogether, with Ramirez calling for all detained immigrants to be released within six months.

The bill would repeal the major detention authorities outlined in immigration law, end contracts with major detention facilities, and ban future spending on immigration detention and monitoring programs. ICE's existing ankle monitor program would end, with all immigrants currently being monitored having their devices removed.

Under the proposal, the construction of the border wall would be halted, while the Border Patrol's integrated surveillance tower program would be terminated.

Some agencies would be moved elsewhere within the federal government, with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) falling under a new Department of Community Safety.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and the U.S. Coast Guard would move to the Department of Transportation, and the Treasury would take care of CBP's customs and trade-related duties.

As for immigration enforcement, that would be dealt with by the Department of Justice, while CBP facilities at the border would be used as effective welcome centers for asylum seekers to meet social workers, medical professionals, and interpreters.

"America’s brave ICE agents put their lives on the line every day to enforce U.S. law and arrest criminal illegal aliens—including gang members, rapists, and murderers. Representative Ramirez should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district—NOT vilifying law enforcement," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek Tuesday. "This type of rhetoric is contributing to a more than 1,300% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line."

Why the Bill Matters Now

The proposal arrives as Republicans continue to campaign heavily on border security and illegal immigration, issues which have repeatedly ranked among voters' top concerns in recent years.

Political analysts have long pointed to immigration as one of the GOP's strongest issues, while Democrats have struggled to reach a consensus on the issue in recent years.

While tackling illegal immigration was an issue that helped reelect President Donald Trump in 2024, the president has seen support waver over the past year amid violent clashes between federal agents and American citizens, as well as sweeping arrests of immigrants without legal status who do not have other criminal records.

Trump has even seen some Republicans begin to break away from the GOP's core message on immigration, as they see constituents who voted red in 2024 grow concerned about the arrests of their loved ones or neighbors.

Who Is Supporting the Bill?

Ramirez has so far been joined by three other Democrats as cosponsors on the bill:

Rashida Tlaib of Michigan

Adelita Grijalva of Arizona

Jim McGovern of Massachusetts

The legislation is also supported by a number of immigrant rights advocacy groups and progressive advocacy organizations, including National Nurses United, Indivisible Chicago Alliance, Center for Constitutional Rights, Defending Rights & Dissent, Bend the Arc, and U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights Action.

Regardless of whether the bill advances legislatively, it is likely to generate debate over immigration and border security as parties battle for control of Congress in November.

title: Immigration, climate, guns: key Trump policies to be tested at supreme court - The Guardian
description:
In 2018, officials in Boulder, Colorado, sued ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, alleging damages to the state’s environment from burning fossil fuels.
ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy argued the lawsuit was incorrectly brought in state court instead of federal court.
The case could potentially end in a 4-4 split because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself, citing a conflict of interest.
The supreme court will examine whether a lower court judge had the authority to pause the quick deportations and if the policy itself violates law, the constitution or international law.
Already, the court handed Trump a victory in the dispute by allowing officials to temporarily deport immigrants to third countries while legal proceedings continue.
text:
1. Suncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County

The case centers on a question raised in dozens of similar lawsuits: how can states, cities or counties hold energy companies accountable for contributing to climate change through fossil fuel burning.

In 2018, officials in Boulder, Colorado, sued ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, alleging damages to the state’s environment from burning fossil fuels.

ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy argued the lawsuit was incorrectly brought in state court instead of federal court. Justices are being asked to decide if the lawsuit can move forward.

The case could potentially end in a 4-4 split because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself, citing a conflict of interest.

2. Rhoney v Barbosa da Cunha

The case is a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of indefinitely detaining immigrants who are arrested in the US and awaiting deportation.

Previously, undocumented immigrants who had been living in the US could be released back into their communities on bond, as long as they did not pose a threat to safety nor were considered a flight risk. But last year, the administration reinterpreted the statute to mean any migrant who entered the US illegally should be held in detention while awaiting legal proceedings.

The reinterpretation has led to a huge surge in the number of migrants held in detention centers and disputes in lower courts.

3. Department of Homeland Security v DVD

The case focuses on the Trump administration’s swift deportations of immigrants to “third countries”, or countries other than their own, without allowing them to contest their removals.

The administration has entered into a series of agreements with other countries that have agreed to safely accept immigrants who cannot be deported to their home countries. But several immigrants say they were not given sufficient “notice and opportunity” to raise concerns about fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they are being sent.

The supreme court will examine whether a lower court judge had the authority to pause the quick deportations and if the policy itself violates law, the constitution or international law.

Already, the court handed Trump a victory in the dispute by allowing officials to temporarily deport immigrants to third countries while legal proceedings continue.

4. St Mary Catholic Parish v Roy

The case is the latest example of the clash between states’ anti-discrimination laws and religious organizations’ right to exercise their values.

Two Catholic parishes say their preschools were precluded from participating in a state-funded universal pre-school program because it required them to sign a nondiscrimination agreement that prevented them from denying admission to families who do not align with Catholic values – such as same-sex couples.

The Catholic parishes requested an exemption, which was denied.

They say it violated their first amendment right because it excluded them from receiving state benefits that were “generally available”, and other pre-schools received exemptions, such as only admitting low-income families or children with disabilities.

The conservative majority of the court has been largely sympathetic to plaintiffs in similar disputes, such as allowing a Colorado baker to refuse to create wedding cakes for same-sex couples.

5. Viramontes v Cook County & Grant v Higgins

The consolidated cases serve as a vehicle for justices to expand access to semi-automatic firearms, such as AR-15-style rifles, by striking down state or local bans on the types of weapons.

Residents of Cook county, Illinois, challenged a county ordinance banning the sale, transfer or possession of any “assault weapon” – which AR-15-style rifles fall under. Separately, a group of Connecticut residents challenged a similar state law that was enacted after the Sandy Hook elementary school shooting.

Lawyers in the cases argue that banning AR-15s is unconstitutional because they are common-use firearms.

In recent years, the supreme court has expanded second amendment protections. In 2022, the court created a new test, requiring courts and legislators to determine whether a gun law conflicted with the United States’ “history and tradition” of firearm ownership.

6. Republican National Committee v Mi Familia Vota

The case centers on two Arizona laws, one requiring voter applicants to provide proof of citizenship, another allowing election officials to remove people believed to be noncitizens from voter rolls 90 days before an election.

Voting advocacy groups argue the laws, enacted in 2022, violate the National Voter Registration Act.

Donald Trump has long called for federal ID requirements and voter roll regulations to address his debunked claims of mass noncitizen fraud in elections.

While a ruling in the case would not impact federal law, it could open the door for states to enact their own voter ID rules.

title: Civil rights advocates plan to send thousands of observers to midterm polling places | WLRN
description:
For many election cycles, groups have fanned out to monitor polling places, but the charged midterm environment has many organizations stepping up efforts.
Chiefly, groups say they are worried about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, agents at election sites.
READ MORE: Palm Beach voters’ guide banned, then restored to libraries It would be illegal for the Trump administration to send armed agents to polling sites.
And leaders of the Justice Department, which regularly monitors polling places, say they plan to step up their usual presence.
Harmeet Dhillon, the head of DOJ's Civil Rights Division, said on Real America's Voice that she plans to send a thousand people from the agency to monitor polling sites.
text:
It was loteria night at the offices of Living United for Change in Arizona, or LUCHA, in Phoenix.

A small group of young people were playing this bingo-like card game in the hopes of taking home an array of prizes: a camping chair, reusable water bottles and coolers.

Conveniently, the prizes would be useful if you plan to camp out somewhere for a while. Which happens to be what these players were getting trained to do last week.

LUCHA, a left-of-center community organizing group, has been training volunteers to be what they call "constitutional observers" ahead of this year's midterms. This was the first of many in-person sessions the organization plans to hold as Election Day nears.

Carime Rodriguez, who led the training, told volunteers that their main job will be to just observe.

"Monitor the polling environment," she said. "Stay aware of what's happening on the ground … just make sure you are kind of keeping your eyes open."

For many election cycles, groups have fanned out to monitor polling places, but the charged midterm environment has many organizations stepping up efforts. They plan to have thousands of individuals with eyes on this election.

Fears of ICE at the polls

For LUCHA's Rodriguez, immigration is a concern. She told her training volunteers that during Arizona's primaries earlier this year, there was an uptick in immigration enforcement — including around polling sites in Maricopa County, where Phoenix is located.

And in case this happens again, LUCHA and other similar groups want to have people on the ground, to keep an eye out for anything they think could intimidate voters. Chiefly, groups say they are worried about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, agents at election sites.

"I feel like these last two years, everyone has been holding on by the edge of their seats," said Alejandra Gomez, LUCHA's executive director. "And so that has made us incredibly forward thinking and making sure that we are preparing. We're hoping for the best, preparing for the worst."

READ MORE: Palm Beach voters’ guide banned, then restored to libraries

It would be illegal for the Trump administration to send armed agents to polling sites. And administration officials have said ICE has no plans to target polling locations. But right-wing political figures close to Trump like Steven Bannon have been calling for the president to send them anyway, and Trump officials have said ICE could serve warrants at polling places.

Mary Corcoran, co-founder and executive director of the left-leaning Save America Movement, said that's enough for her to take this potential threat seriously.

"The point is to scare people and use fear as an intimidation factor to keep people home," she told NPR. "So, our perspective was that the way that we could make a difference in this election was working in communities that would be most likely impacted by the threat of ICE coming to the polls this fall."

Corcoran's group is partnering with the Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network, as well as various unions, like the American Federation of Teachers, in an effort they are calling Vote Safe.

She said members of the effort plan to be in major population centers with large and growing Black, Latino, Asian and immigrant populations — particularly in states with key Senate races, like Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia and Michigan.

"The volunteers are not there to engage with any ICE folks that could show up," she said. "It's really about having a de-escalatory impact by way of really bearing witness."

She said the presence of clergy, veterans, teachers and nurses from the community will hopefully have a "de-escalatory impact and a deterrent impact."

DOJ election observers

Left-leaning groups won't be the only folks at the polls. The Republican National Committee, for one, recruits observers to keep elections secure and transparent. And leaders of the Justice Department, which regularly monitors polling places, say they plan to step up their usual presence.

Harmeet Dhillon, the head of DOJ's Civil Rights Division, said on Real America's Voice that she plans to send a thousand people from the agency to monitor polling sites.

"This is going to be the biggest DOJ election observer effort in history," she said. "And I'm so excited to be leading that effort."

She said that DOJ staff will play a similar role to other observers that will be at the polls, which is just to watch.

"They're not going to be interfering in any way or running the election, they're going to be observing, making notes," she said.

Wyoming's Republican governor criticized the actions of DOJ observers in the state in August.

"Not normal times"

Tammy Patrick with the National Association of Election Officials says election administrators have been hearing of big plans of large groups of observers for a while now. But Patrick said it's important to note that this is something they hear most election cycles.

"Every two years it seems, for at least the 20 or so years I've been doing this, we hear that there's going to be massive observation, and thousands of people are going to show up to observe at the polling place," she said.

"It hasn't manifested in that way in the past, but these are not normal times."

Which is why she says election administrators are educating the public. Rules about who can observe what, or how close you can be to a polling site, for example, vary from state to state.

Also, there is only so much observers can actually do at the polls. If something goes wrong, it's up to election workers and local law enforcement to sort it out.

Patrick said most years many observers get bored and leave.

"The actual process tends to be ... pretty dry," she said. "And one might even say boring to watch people walk in, give their name, sign their name, get their ballot."

But if things are not boring, Jane Kleeb with the Association of State Democratic Committees — which is part of the Democratic National Committee — said she wants people on the ground recording.

For political parties, the stakes of problems at the polls are high — particularly in close elections, where lawsuits are common.

text:
The Trump administration is unlawfully confiscating the personal property of detained immigrants and thus setting them up for failure upon their release, a new lawsuit filed in federal court claims.

Since January 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has "routinely failed to return important items seized from people detained for civil immigration purposes after releasing them," the lawsuit alleges. Such property includes government-issued documents like driver's licenses, passports and employment authorization documents, as well as items like money, jewelry, cellphones, car keys and clothing, according to the filing.

In a 39-page complaint, several immigrants who have had their property confiscated since President Donald Trump took office say ICE's behavior in this regard is unlawful because it violates internal agency rules, federal statutory law and the U.S. Constitution.

"ICE has a de facto policy of failing to return property seized from people detained for civil immigration purposes, depriving people of their property long after any legitimate governmental interest in the property has expired," the lawsuit begins. "ICE has deprived people of such items for far longer than any conceivable governmental interest would justify, often months after the individuals were released from ICE custody."

While the plaintiffs do not suggest there is any statute outright barring ICE agents from confiscating such property, the lawsuit argues the de facto policy violates the agency's actual confiscation and detention policies, the Fourth Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the federal statute that governs the behavior of administrative agencies.

"The upshot is this: The De Facto Policy, whether applied to documents or any other form of property, is unlawful several times over," the lawsuit goes on. "Plaintiffs … seek the return of items that ICE unlawfully failed to return to them as well as safeguards to prevent ICE from continuing to unreasonably deny people their property."

In a post on X (formerly Twitter) announcing the litigation, attorney Norm Eisen termed the policy "a cruel catch-22."

The lawsuit says it describes "seven people who fell victim" to the de facto policy after they were detained and released.

"At least five months have passed since each Plaintiff was released from ICE custody, and all Plaintiffs are still missing important property, despite requesting its return," the filing alleges.

The plaintiffs claim they have been negatively financially affected by the government holding onto the belongings in question.

On top of expending "significant resources to replace or regain their possessions," several plaintiffs have lost their jobs due to the lack of identification or work authorization, according to the complaint.

The filing makes clear the allegations against ICE are nothing new.

"Across the country, federal judges have held government officials in contempt, or threatened to do so, due to ICE's failure to return items that had been seized from people released from ICE detention," the complaint goes on. "Journalists and immigration lawyers have reported a similar practice."

In September, U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher, a Trump appointee, found numerous violations of court orders in a habeas corpus case filed by an underage immigrant. In that case, she ordered the government to return all of the "property and documents that were removed from his person at the time of his wrongful removal."

In the present case, the plaintiffs insist ICE is violating its own policies when it refuses to surrender lawfully seized documents.

"The De Facto Policy demonstrates how ICE has operationalized the Confiscation Directive and shows that the agency treats it as authorizing officers to choose whether to return seized documents," the lawsuit goes on. "Properly read, however, the Confiscation Directive does not authorize such conduct. Instead, the Confiscation Directive states that ICE's enforcement officers … must '[e]nsur[e] that decisions to retain documents are based on a clearly articulated operational need.'"

In other words, the plaintiffs allege the government no longer has any viable "need" to retain such property after an immigrant is released.

This alleged lack of need dovetails with the APA argument. The plaintiffs allege the lack of need makes ICE's behavior arbitrary and capricious, a term of art derived from the APA's originating statute — which refers to agency actions that go too far while eschewing formal, mandatory processes.

But the lawsuit also stakes out even broader territory to argue the de facto policy is "unconstitutional."

"To the extent that the Confiscation Directive did indeed authorize ICE to retain documents in these scenarios, it would be unlawful under the Fourth Amendment," the plaintiffs claim.

The lawsuit seeks class certification and an injunction.

The plaintiffs not only hope to regain all of their confiscated property, but to force ICE to return such property throughout the country — and to stop the policy from being acted upon in the future.
