text:
HOUSTON — A man who was injured when an ICE officer’s car ran over him has had surgery on his leg but needs additional procedures to reconstruct the leg and other parts of his body, an advocate for the man said Monday.

Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, had leg and hip injuries and a shattered ankle after the officer’s vehicle struck him during a pursuit Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, a co-founder and the executive director of FIEL, who was speaking on Parra’s behalf. Parra cannot put weight on his leg for six weeks and must wait for swelling to reduce before doctors can perform additional surgery, he said at a news conference Monday.

Espinosa said Parra — who had gotten out of a vehicle and was on foot — was hit “in a violent and brutal fashion.”

ICE has said it attempted a vehicle stop and the people in the car ran away. The officers tried to apprehend the fleeing men, and “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck,” it said.

It has said Parra was not the target of the attempted stop.

Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

Video obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. The video shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in the shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not respond to a request for further comment.

Parra was at a Houston area hospital Monday morning when his attorney and Espinosa visited him, Espinosa said. But they had only 10 or 15 minutes before ICE officers came in and began recording their conversation and forced them out, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said.

“To add insult to injury, Mr. Miguel is in the custody of the ICE agents who ran him down,” Espinosa said. “This is so disheartening and so angering that Miguel has to face the people that brutally attacked them every single day, 24 hours a day.”

Parra has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and he has no criminal record, Bruno told NBC News. DHS said he was in the country without legal permission.

Bruno said he has never had encounters with immigration authorities. He and the man with him in the car do stucco work, she said.

Neither Parra nor the other man in the car was the target of ICE in Saturday’s traffic stop, Bruno and Espinosa said.

ICE identified the man it was targeting as Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who it said is not legally in the country and had been removed twice and entered the U.S. illegally five times. It said that Mendoza Cervantes had been arrested multiple times for drunken driving and once for unlawful possession of a firearm and that he had an active removal order.

Bruno and Espinosa countered that neither Parra nor the man in the car with him, whom he had picked up for work, knew Mendoza Cervantes.

The Civil Rights Division of the Harris County District Attorney’s Office sent investigators to the intersection where Parra was hit, said Damali Keith, a spokesman for the district attorney’s office.

text:
In his first televised interview since a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot Oscar Bergal in New York City last week, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff that during a nearly two-hour phone call with President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, he demanded the agency cease its operations in the city. Mamdani said ICE’s actions were “making a mockery of what law and order is supposed to be” and leaving residents in a “state of terror.”

Bergal, a 28-year-old Dominican national — whose last name has also been reported as “Belgal” — was shot in the neck while sitting in a car with his 5-year-old son during an attempted arrest Thursday afternoon in Marble Hill, a neighborhood in northern Manhattan. Federal officials have defended the operation, citing Bergal’s criminal history and alleged gang affiliations.

According to Mamdani, Thursday’s shooting was yet another example of ICE’s disregard of protocol. “What they have shown, time and again, is that they view the law as a suggestion,” he said. “There is a reason why the NYPD would not be shooting at a moving vehicle. There is a reason why law enforcement agents are supposed to wear identifiable information and uniforms.”

Mamdani said bystanders witnessed a scene that looked more like a mass shooting than a law enforcement operation. “We’re talking about people carrying their shopping bags, walking by a bodega, thinking they’re on their way home, then they hear shots ring out. And they don’t even know whether this is from someone who is supposed to be a law enforcement agent or just someone who is terrorizing the city,” he said. “And when it comes to ICE, there is no difference between those two things.”

Asked whether the city would pursue criminal charges against the agent who fired, Mamdani told Soboroff that local authorities were investigating. “Right now, this case is with District Attorney Clark in the Bronx, and I am fully confident in the district attorney,” he said.

Mamdani also discussed his nearly two-hour call with Trump and Mullin shortly after the shooting, during which he said he pressed the administration to end its immigration operations in New York City.

“I’ve said directly to the president, I’ve said directly to the secretary, as someone who cares about public safety, who cares about law and order, I am demanding that ICE cease their operations in our city immediately,” he said. “Because these operations make New Yorkers less safe. They leave New Yorkers in a state of terror, and that is something that should be opposed by all of us.”

More articles

Mamdani said he told Trump that public safety was one of his “top priorities” and argued that ICE’s presence undermined that goal. “It is from that concern that I believe that ICE should not be in this city at all,” the mayor said. “ICE should, frankly, not even be an agency that exists, because what we see from their actions is an agency that terrorizes, one that creates a sense of fear, as opposed to any idea of safety.”

Soboroff asked if, given that the mayor has met and spoken by phone with the president on several occasions since he returned to the White House, Mamdani believed his “cordial“ relationship with Trump had helped the city. Mamdani pointed to the release of a New York City college student from ICE detention after an earlier meeting but acknowledged that his negotiations after the shooting of Bergal had not produced the outcome he wanted.

“Those two hours over the course of Thursday evening, those negotiations, they were ultimately unsuccessful,” Mamdani said. “However, I would be betraying my duty as the mayor of our city if I did not try at every single juncture with every single person to keep this city safe, and that is something that I will always continue to do.”

“A willingness to negotiate should never be understood as a willingness to surrender our principles,” he said.

You can watch Soboroff’s full interview with Mamdani in the clip at the top of the page.

title: Rep. Omar accuses Trump of political intimidation after agents search her home - PBS
description:
Geoff Bennett: Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Minnesota Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar early this morning.
Devlin Barrett, The New York Times: So, Geoff, the Trump administration has been signaling just such a move for months now.
Geoff Bennett: And, of course, we're talking about federal agents searching the home of a sitting member of Congress.
Geoff Bennett: What would legal experts look for to distinguish a legitimate criminal investigation from one driven by political motivations?
Geoff Bennett: Devlin Barrett of The New York Times and the author of the book "The Department of Revenge: How Trump Took Control of American Justice."
text:
Geoff Bennett:

Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Minnesota Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar early this morning. The reason for the search has not been made public. Agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative arm of ICE, were seen carrying boxes from the home into an unmarked car.

Omar accused the Trump administration of political intimidation, writing on social media -- quote -- "Make no mistake, this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

For more, we're joined now by Devlin Barrett, Justice Department reporter for The New York Times and author of the book "The Department of Revenge: How Trump Took Control of American Justice."

Devlin, always great to have you with us.

So the DOJ says this search is part of an ongoing criminal investigation. What have you learned about what prompted it and what investigators are looking for?

Devlin Barrett, The New York Times:

So, Geoff, the Trump administration has been signaling just such a move for months now. If you go back to the spring, J.D. Vance, the vice president, said that Ilhan Omar -- quote -- "definitely committed immigration fraud."

And DHS officials have since said they're investigating. So this move isn't much of a surprise, but I think it does speak to the way that law enforcement actions keep happening at the at the impetus and prodding of the White House.

And what's at issue here, according to our sources, is all the paperwork in the congresswoman's family that led them to becoming U.S. citizens. That's paperwork that her father filled out, paperwork that was done later. And what they're investigating is false statements on immigration documents potentially and various types of fraud and conspiracy.

Geoff Bennett:

A federal judge had to approve this search warrant, so what does that suggest about the evidence investigators presented? Would it have been the sort of documents that you're talking about?

Devlin Barrett:

Right.

So they have to show probable cause to believe that evidence of this crime or possible crimes existed at her house. And probable cause is not the same thing as the amount of evidence it takes a jury to convict. We are told by sources that prosecutors first applied for this search warrant more than a week ago.

And that led to a back-and-forth with a federal judge over whether they had shown enough of a legal argument for why they needed to do this and whether they had considered the issues related to the constitutional protections that are specific to a lawmaker.

Geoff Bennett:

And, of course, we're talking about federal agents searching the home of a sitting member of Congress. How extraordinary is that? What safeguards are supposed to govern an investigation this sensitive?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, the federal government does investigate lawmakers all the time. That's not particularly unusual.

What's so unusual here is that they're doing it 22 days before an election, because the Justice Department has for many years followed something called a 60-day rule, which is basically meant to go quiet, make the Justice Department go quiet about things exactly like searches of lawmakers' homes and businesses, because they don't want to be seen as trying to influence the election.

Here, what you see is a very publicly observable, overt act of investigation that past administrations would have done everything they could to try to avoid doing just before an election.

Geoff Bennett:

What would legal experts look for to distinguish a legitimate criminal investigation from one driven by political motivations?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, it's things like, what is the basis of the evidence that leads you to probable cause?

Obviously, a judge has determined that there is some probable cause here. And -- but, at the same time, we also know that there was the judge didn't immediately accept that application, that there was some back-and-forth before they got to this point.

I think one of the ways in which the Trump administration sort of creates its own headaches and its own problems when it comes to criminal investigations is, remember how this process began. It began with the vice president of the United States publicly declaring her to be guilty.

And there's obviously a long history of the president himself, Donald Trump, accusing Ilhan Omar of various things. So the challenge that will -- that the government will have to overcome if it proceeds to try to charge her is overcoming questions or skepticism about, what was the motivation behind this investigation?

Geoff Bennett:

And when you say if the government proceeds, what would come next in this investigation?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, if they decide they have enough evidence that they can get an indictment, then they would present their evidence to a grand jury.

What's going to happen now is, after -- now that there's been a search and we have seen agents taking away boxes of evidence, they're going to have to sort through everything they have taken. And there may be some fights, legal fights, to come over what of that evidence that is seized is properly part of the investigation.

And so we don't know if there's going to be a legal fight over that. I wouldn't be surprised if there is. But the next prosecutorial step, assuming that they know what evidence they have and they believe it would survive a vote in a grand jury, would be to present the evidence to a grand jury.

Geoff Bennett:

Devlin Barrett of The New York Times and the author of the book "The Department of Revenge: How Trump Took Control of American Justice."

Devlin, always a pleasure to speak with you. Thanks.

Devlin Barrett:

Thanks, Geoff.

text:
In the mode of historic fascist regimes, President Donald Trump’s administration sent federal agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to raid the home of a political opponent, singled out for her race and religion, in a transparent effort to strip her of her citizenship.

On Monday, agents with Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing, conducted a search of the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., with federal officials describing the incursion as part of “an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

HSI was previously known for targeting human traffickers, drug smugglers, and war criminals. But under the second Trump administration, the unit has been increasingly focused on investigating protesters and immigration fraud.

That latter category is exactly what Trump administration officials have been prejudiciously applying to Omar for months. In March, Vice President JD Vance said, “We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.”

And, last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that “something is going to happen” on the Omar case, with immigration czar Tom Homan confirming an investigation.

The ICE raid against Omar, however, is an extremist escalation in Trump’s long-running threats to denaturalize the member of Congress, who was born in Somalia but came to the U.S. as a refugee when she was a young child. Omar, who has denied the repeated allegations of immigration fraud, is on the ballot for reelection in November.

Not only does the raid send a chill to all naturalized citizens who, like Omar, oppose the Trump regime, it is also one of the most ominous signs to date of how dangerous Trump and his acolytes can get in the next two years.

With his popularity tanking and his grip on power growing tenuous, Trump is becoming a flailing tyrant. Meanwhile, he has been granted extraordinary executive power by a loyalist Supreme Court and has purged the federal government of practically all checks and balances. It’s a recipe for immense harm.

A Nakedly Fascist Move

Debates about whether the Trump regime qualifies as fascist are old, tired, and not worth retreading here.

There can be little doubt, though, that targeting a racialized political opponent for deportation three weeks before an election is a nakedly fascist move — especially in the context of the far right’s evermore vitriolic attacks on Somali communities nationwide.

“Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post last week. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”

It was nothing short of an exhortation to a race war.

As his popular support continues to wane, we can be sure that the president and his white supremacist Cabinet will marshal the force of the federal government in even more fascistic ways.

Many means of stopping Trump have been defanged, as the raid itself makes clear.

We cannot rely on the courts. The warrant to search Omar’s home, for instance, was signed by a judge.

The judicial system, indeed, has permitted vast swaths of Trump’s anti-immigrant excesses. Courts have also sent activists to prison for decades for attending protests against the federal government. And, while some federal judges and even the Supreme Court have pushed back on some of Trump’s agenda, it is also the courts that have covered the president with impunity. We know, too, that this administration routinely disregards court orders in the knowledge that it will not face consequences.

There is little more optimism to be had on the congressional front. Even if Democrats take back Congress in November, they must reckon with an embattled authoritarian executive with a fully funded standing militia — namely, ICE.

Democrats should unite to stop Trump’s efforts to lawlessly deport a colleague based on a racist political witch hunt, but we can expect little congressional action beyond condemnatory statements. Indeed, all too many centrist Democrats have been happy to throw left-wing colleagues, particularly Muslims like Omar and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., to the wolves.

Elected leaders, from the national to municipal level, should be strategizing about how to protect their constituents from Trump’s worst extremes in the knowledge that he and his allies will escalate further. Impeachment should be a priority, yes, but so too should passing laws to dismantle and defund ICE, among other measures — just the sorts of things mainstream Democrats have refused to countenance.

If not the courts or elected leaders, what then? The answer is clear: Trump’s desperate authoritarianism must also be met by mass popular and militant opposition.

It is not enough to vote in November, then cross our fingers for two more years. Organizers on the front lines defending immigrant neighbors against ICE are exhausted and need numbers and support.

Activists facing trial or already sentenced to decades in prison for resisting Trump’s regime need ongoing legal support and funding. Readiness is all.

This is not to suggest that we must live in a state of paralyzing fear of an evermore delusional tyrant. The point, rather, is to recognize the danger and go on.

Resistance to Trump, to the border regime, and to racist state violence already exists; it must be supported, expanded, and the subject of an escalation of our own.

text:
Federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat.

Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump.

A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years.

MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November’s midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.

Fox News, which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child.

Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar’s home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning.

Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.

Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday.

The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, “Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.”

“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation,” the DOJ said.

Omar’s spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, “This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.”

“For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back,” Rogers said. “Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies.”

In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family’s immigration to the United States.

“There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with,” said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.

The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.

The person familiar with the raid on Omar’s home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.

Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates “solid Democrat.” The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.

The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid.

“The Trump administration’s raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries,” said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, the Democratic Caucus chair, in a statement.

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” the statement said. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”

“The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice.”

The Justice Department confirmed in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area in connection with an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.

The nature and scope of the investigation were unclear, though officials in President Donald Trump's administration have repeatedly hinted at the existence of an inquiry targeting Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have repeatedly drawn criticism from Republicans and senior Trump officials.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that there was an "ongoing investigation" related in part to whether Omar lied on her immigration forms and that "something's going to happen."

Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search of her home took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot for reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.

"For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," top House Democratic leaders said in a statement. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.

Trump has frequently targeted Omar

Trump and fellow Republicans from the highest ranks of party leadership have repeatedly and publicly criticized the Somali-born Omar over her status as an immigrant to the U.S. and her left-wing views. Trump as recently as this past weekend brought up Omar at a rally in Tennessee, where he attacked her upbringing and suggested that Vice President JD Vance "and our people" were investigating her.

Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud — an allegation she has denied — and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate her.

The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area but provided no other details. The street was blocked off Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home.

"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the department said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department.

Omar has long been a target for Republicans

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota's 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.

In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced recently to 14 months in prison.

Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies."

"It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance told reporters in May. "So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime."

In a separate interview with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that "we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America."

He said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had been discussing it and "trying to look at what the remedies are."

"That's the thing that we're trying to figure out," he said. "What are the legal remedies now that we know that she's committed immigration fraud. How do you go after her? How do you investigate her? How do you actually do the thing? How do you build the case necessary to get some, some, some justice for the American people?"

Omar's office has defended her against past allegations

Omar's office in March dismissed Vance's claims as fabricated and defamatory.

"This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to 'create stories' to redirect the media," Omar's chief of staff, Connor McNutt, said in a statement.

"This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party's unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers," McNutt said at the time of the vice president's allegations and comments.

Associated Press writers Lisa Mascaro, Michelle L. Price and River Zhang in Washington, Kathy McCormack in Concord, N.H., Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pa., and Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., contributed.

title: The Supreme Court's Trump Emergency Docket Advantage—and Where It Disappears
description:
Across the emergency applications examined here, Trump has an apparent advantage when his administration seeks relief.
To separate these relationships, this analysis examines Supreme Court emergency applications involving general federal executive actions from January 20, 2017, through October 12, 2026.
The relatively small number of Biden applications, however, limits how precisely the magnitude of that advantage can be estimated.
Among substantively decided government-applicant applications, Trump prevailed in 11 of 12 immigration matters during his first term, or 92%.
In March 2020, the first Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay a lower-court injunction restricting the program.
text:
Share

In August 2024, the Biden administration asked the Supreme Court to partially lift lower-court injunctions blocking its new Title IX regulations, which expanded protections against sex discrimination in education and the justices refused. Less than eight months later, the Trump administration asked the same Court to intervene after a federal judge ordered the Department of Education to continue funding grants it had terminated. This time, the government prevailed.

Both applications came from the Department of Education, both sought emergency relief from lower-court orders, and both were decided by the same nine justices. Yet the outcomes differed. The comparison invites a broader question about the Supreme Court’s treatment of presidential power: Does the Court give Donald Trump a more favorable reception than Joe Biden? The two cases also illustrate why answering that question is difficult. They concerned different policies, legal claims, and procedural circumstances, each of which could influence how the justices responded.

Across the emergency applications examined here, Trump has an apparent advantage when his administration seeks relief. During his first term, the government prevailed in 28 of 36 substantively decided applications, or 78%, in the published full-term tally. During his second term, the figure rises to 27 of 33, or 82%. Under Biden, it was 10 of 15, or 67%. But that difference becomes considerably smaller when the comparison expands to include cases in which the government was defending its actions against applications filed by others. At the level of distinct controversies, executive success was approximately 75% under Trump I, 74% under Biden, and 77% under Trump II. The choice of what to compare therefore makes a considerable difference in how presidential success appears.

Part of the explanation is visible in the composition of the docket. Immigration accounts for 12 identified government-applicant applications during Trump’s first term and 14 during his second, compared with four under Biden. Trump’s second-term docket also includes 10 personnel and removal applications involving presidential control over executive-branch officials and operations. Biden’s affirmative applications were more concentrated in education and public health, while Trump’s first-term docket featured a larger share of immigration, federal execution litigation, foreign-affairs, and census disputes. Comparing the administrations therefore also means comparing different mixtures of executive actions, legal disputes, and lower-court interventions.

To separate these relationships, this analysis examines Supreme Court emergency applications involving general federal executive actions from January 20, 2017, through October 12, 2026. The primary dataset contains 165 identified applications grouped into 109 distinct controversies, with 93 controversies producing determinate outcomes. Applications are classified by administration, whether the federal government sought or opposed emergency relief, substantive issue, policy direction, lower-court circumstances, and disposition. Related applications are grouped into controversies so that repeated litigation over a single executive policy does not disproportionately influence the aggregate results. Applications withdrawn, dismissed as moot, deferred, or otherwise unresolved are excluded from the success-rate calculations. Individual justice positions are reconstructed from the Court’s orders, treating justices who did not actively dissent as joining the Court’s disposition. The published first-term Trump tally includes three favorable rulings not yet linked to records in the case-level file; those rulings are not assigned individual issue classifications or justice positions.

The key question is how much of Trump’s advantage survives closer comparisons. Does the difference persist when the government is the party requesting relief, when the same substantive issue is involved, or when the Court confronts similar lower-court restrictions? Do particular policies receive greater support regardless of who occupies the White House? And do individual justices consistently favor presidential authority, or does their support change with the administration and the substance of its actions? Examining these distinctions provides a more precise account of presidential success on the emergency docket than the overall win rates alone.

A Presidential Advantage That Depends on Who Is Asking

The first important distinction in comparing Trump and Biden is the position each administration occupied when its disputes reached the Supreme Court. During both Trump presidencies, the federal government overwhelmingly appeared as the applicant, asking the justices to intervene after a lower-court ruling had restricted an executive action. Under Biden, the pattern was nearly reversed. His administration was much more frequently defending an existing policy against an emergency application brought by someone else.

The difference is substantial. Of the 39 core applications involving Trump’s first administration, the government was the applicant in 34. Under Trump II, it was the applicant in 42 of 45. Under Biden, the government brought only 18 of 81 applications; the other 63 were brought by challengers to federal executive action. These figures describe the full core dataset, including applications subsequently withdrawn or otherwise resolved without a substantive ruling. They show that the administrations reached the Court through markedly different litigation pathways.

That difference changes what an executive victory means. When the government files an emergency application, success generally requires persuading the justices to disturb a lower-court ruling. When the government is the respondent, success may mean convincing the Court to deny the challenger’s application, allowing the existing policy or lower-court arrangement to remain in place. Those outcomes both favor the executive, but the Court is being asked to exercise its emergency authority in different directions.

The difference becomes apparent in the outcomes. Among applications in which the federal government sought relief and the Court issued a substantive disposition, Trump prevailed in 25 of 33 identified applications during his first term (76%), and in 28 of 36 (78%) under the published full-term tally, which includes three additional favorable rulings. He prevailed in 27 of 33 during his second term (82%). Biden prevailed in 10 of 15 (67%). The Trump administrations therefore had a higher success rate when seeking emergency intervention, with the difference especially pronounced during Trump’s second term. The relatively small number of Biden applications, however, limits how precisely the magnitude of that advantage can be estimated.

The comparison looks different when every distinct executive-action controversy receives equal weight, regardless of which side requested relief or how many applications the controversy generated. The executive prevailed in 18 of 24 determinate Trump I controversies (75%), 29 of 39 Biden controversies (74%), and 23 of 30 Trump II controversies (77%). At this level, the three administrations look remarkably similar. Biden’s overall record is considerably stronger than his applicant-only record because his administration frequently prevailed when challengers sought to interfere with its policies. Among the determinate Biden controversies initiated by challengers, the executive prevailed in 21 of 27, or 78%.

The two comparisons capture different dimensions of the Court’s behavior. Trump enjoyed greater success securing affirmative emergency relief, while Biden’s frequent success defending executive actions brought his overall record close to those of both Trump administrations. The distinction is important, although it leaves the central explanation unresolved. The presidents did not arrive with interchangeable applications, and the legal burden of obtaining emergency intervention depends on more than the identity of the applicant. The next question is therefore what kinds of executive actions each administration was bringing before the justices.

Three Administrations, Three Different Emergency Dockets

The presidential comparison becomes more revealing when the applications are separated by subject matter. Trump and Biden approached the same Supreme Court with substantially different portfolios of disputes, reflecting differences in executive policy, the lower-court challenges those policies encountered, and the kinds of relief each administration sought. These differences help explain why overall success rates can conceal important distinctions in the Court’s treatment of presidential actions.

Across the 94 identified core applications filed by the federal government, immigration is the largest recurring category under both Trump administrations. During Trump’s first term, 12 of 34 government applications concerned immigration, citizenship, or border policy. Eight more involved federal execution litigation, with seven favorable dispositions for the government, while foreign-affairs and elections/census disputes accounted for four applications each. The first Trump administration’s emergency docket was therefore heavily concentrated in questions involving entry restrictions, immigration enforcement, federal executions, and other exercises of federal authority. These government applications generally sought to lift lower-court restrictions on scheduled federal executions or the execution procedures; they are distinct from the more familiar prisoner-filed applications seeking to halt executions, particularly state executions.

The composition changes during Trump’s second term. Immigration remains prominent, accounting for 14 of 42 government applications, but personnel and removal disputes emerge as a second major category, with 10 applications. Together, those two areas comprise nearly 60% of Trump II’s government-applicant docket. The personnel matters include disputes over presidential authority to remove officials serving on independent federal agencies and the ability of lower courts to reinstate those officials while litigation proceeds. These cases place questions about presidential control of the executive branch more directly before the justices than much of the first-term docket.

Biden’s applicant docket looks different. Of the 18 core applications brought by his administration, five concerned education and five involved health or public-health policy. Those ten applications account for more than half of the government’s affirmative emergency requests. Immigration appears in four applications, but the policies at issue frequently differ in direction from Trump’s. Two additional applications concerned federal firearms regulation, rather than capital punishment. Biden’s education disputes included student-loan programs and Title IX regulations, while his health-related applications included federal vaccination requirements and FDA regulation. The relative prominence of these categories means that comparing presidential success also means comparing very different statutory frameworks and substantive policy choices.

The contrast becomes even more pronounced when the applications filed against each administration are considered. Of the 63 applications in which Biden’s government was the respondent, 25 concerned health or public health and 23 involved environmental or energy regulation. Together, those categories account for approximately three-quarters of the applications challenging Biden-era executive actions. Many arose from repeated challenges to the same policies. The OSHA vaccination-or-testing standard alone generated 15 applications, while several EPA regulations produced additional clusters of related filings.

This distinction between applications and underlying controversies is important. A policy challenged by multiple states or regulated entities can generate several Supreme Court docket numbers, whereas another consequential policy may produce only one application. Accordingly, the application counts reveal how litigation reached the Court, while the controversy-level analysis gives each distinct policy dispute more equal influence when comparing results.

The administrations’ different portfolios provide a plausible explanation for part of the presidential disparity, but they also raise a more precise question. If Trump wins more frequently because his emergency applications involve policies more compatible with the Court’s substantive preferences, we should expect the presidential gap to vary across issue areas. Immigration provides one test, although the administrations often sought opposite policy outcomes. Health, education, and other overlapping categories offer additional comparisons. Examining those differences helps distinguish the Court’s response to a particular president from its response to the legal policies the president asks it to protect.

The Differences Are Clearer Where the Cases Overlap

The different composition of each administration’s emergency docket makes the presidential comparison difficult, but it also provides an opportunity to examine the areas where their cases overlap. If the justices were simply inclined to favor one president over another, we would expect a relatively consistent difference across subject areas. Instead, the size and direction of the presidential advantage change considerably depending on the issue.

Immigration provides the most pronounced contrast. Among substantively decided government-applicant applications, Trump prevailed in 11 of 12 immigration matters during his first term, or 92%. His second administration prevailed in 11 of 12, or 92%. Biden, by comparison, succeeded in two of four, or 50%. These are application-level figures, and related cases sometimes concern the same underlying policy. Nevertheless, they identify immigration as an area in which the Trump administrations achieved considerably greater success than Biden when seeking emergency intervention.

One of the closest comparisons involves the Migrant Protection Protocols, better known as Remain in Mexico. In March 2020, the first Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay a lower-court injunction restricting the program. The justices granted the application, allowing the policy to remain operative while litigation continued. Justice Sotomayor would have denied the request. In August 2021, the Biden administration sought emergency relief from a different injunction requiring continued implementation of the same program after Biden had attempted to terminate it. This time, the Court denied the government’s application, with Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan indicating that they would have granted relief.

The juxtaposition is unusually informative: two presidents, the same federal program, and opposite outcomes when each sought emergency relief. But it also illustrates the importance of the legal question presented. In denying Biden’s application, the Court specifically questioned whether his administration was likely to succeed in defending the explanation it had supplied for rescinding the program under the Administrative Procedure Act. The later merits proceedings further complicate the comparison. In June 2022, the Supreme Court reversed the Fifth Circuit’s judgment and held that federal immigration law did not require the administration to continue Remain in Mexico. The earlier emergency denial therefore cannot be treated as a final judicial endorsement of Trump’s policy over Biden’s.

Other issue areas produce markedly different patterns. Biden prevailed in all four substantively decided health and public-health applications, including challenges involving federal vaccination requirements and FDA regulation. Trump I won one of two such applications, while Trump II won its single substantively decided application in this category. Biden’s success in health disputes stands in contrast to the immigration results and indicates that a general presidential ranking conceals areas in which a Democratic administration received substantial emergency relief.

Education points in the opposite direction. Biden lost all three substantively decided education applications in the core sample, while Trump II won both of its applications. The Biden cases included Title IX and student-loan repayment disputes; Trump’s concerned education grants and executive-branch restructuring. The outcomes differ sharply, although the underlying legal questions provide limited grounds for a direct comparison. Federal execution litigation and firearms regulation offer a different contrast: Biden prevailed in both applications involving the federal ghost-gun rule, while Trump I prevailed in seven of eight applications concerning federal executions. These results arose from substantially different uses of federal authority rather than comparable criminal-law disputes.

The results thus reveal a pattern more complicated than a uniform preference for Trump. His immigration success is substantial, particularly during his first term, but Biden also achieved consistent victories in certain health and firearms disputes. Moreover, the number of genuinely comparable controversies is smaller than the number of applications suggests. Multiple travel-ban applications contribute to the Trump I immigration total, three birthright-citizenship applications contribute to Trump II, and repeated challenges to the same vaccination or firearms rule affect the other categories.

The strongest conclusion from these comparisons is that subject matter makes a difference, although it operates alongside the substantive direction of the policy and the particular relief being requested. The presidential averages combine cases involving different statutes, different lower-court orders, and sometimes opposing positions on the same federal program. To determine whether these differences reflect a general attitude toward executive authority or preferences concerning particular policies, it is necessary to examine how the individual justices respond as the administration changes.

Same Justices, Different Presidents

The presidential comparisons also look different when examined justice by justice. A general preference for executive authority would suggest that at least some justices consistently support the federal government, regardless of which president occupies the White House. The voting patterns reveal something more complicated. Several justices shift dramatically between administrations, while others display considerably more stable support for executive action.

Thomas provides one of the clearest examples. He supported the Trump administration’s position in 83% of the substantively decided applications examined from Trump’s first term and 94% during his second, compared with 41% under Biden. Alito’s corresponding rates were 83%, 94%, and 57%. Sotomayor shows almost the reverse pattern, supporting Biden’s executive position in 93% of applications but Trump’s in 27% during his first term and 11% during his second. Kagan’s support similarly rises to 93% under Biden, compared with 43% under Trump I and 17% under Trump II. Jackson supported the Biden executive position in 89% of her eligible observations, compared with 6% under Trump II.

The differences are considerably smaller for some of the conservative justices. Roberts supported the executive position in 76% of Trump I applications, 73% under Biden, and 78% under Trump II. Kavanaugh’s corresponding figures were 79%, 70%, and 78%. Gorsuch occupied an intermediate position, supporting Trump in 83% of first-term applications and 83% during his second term, compared with 62% under Biden. Barrett’s record is also comparatively balanced, with 75% support under Biden and 78% under Trump II. Her four eligible first-term Trump observations provide too little evidence for a meaningful comparison.

These patterns complicate the proposition that the justices are simply divided between supporters and opponents of strong presidential power. Thomas, Alito, Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson exhibit substantial differences depending on the administration whose position is before them. Roberts and Kavanaugh, by comparison, are relatively consistent across presidents. The variation suggests that support for executive action is associated with the substantive policies and presidential administrations involved, alongside the legal questions presented in individual cases.

The interpretation nevertheless requires care. The figures treat justices who did not publicly dissent as joining the Court’s disposition, so they measure reconstructed voting positions rather than individually recorded votes in every application. They also reflect differences in the cases heard during each presidency, and some justices served for only part of the period. Finally, presidential party and the ideological direction of executive policy often move together in these data, making it difficult to distinguish a justice’s preference for a particular administration from agreement with the policy that administration advances.

The broader finding is that presidential identity alone tells relatively little about aggregate executive success, but it is strongly associated with how several individual justices respond. That contrast helps explain why similar overall success rates can coexist with sharply different patterns of support within the Court. It also limits the explanatory value of a simple strong-executive theory: a justice’s willingness to sustain executive action appears to depend substantially on what the executive is trying to accomplish.

Presidential Power Depending on The President

The Supreme Court’s emergency docket provides evidence of an advantage for Trump, but a more qualified one than the raw outcomes might suggest. Both Trump administrations were more successful than Biden when the federal government requested emergency intervention. Yet when applications are grouped into underlying controversies and cases brought against the government are included, the administrations’ overall success rates converge. Much of the apparent difference depends on whether the president is asking the justices to intervene or defending an action already taken.

The differences also depend substantially on what the administration is trying to accomplish. Trump’s immigration victories contrast with Biden’s success in health-related disputes, while the same justices frequently change their support for executive action across presidencies. Some, particularly Roberts and Kavanaugh, show relatively consistent support for executive positions. Others display sharp differences that align more closely with the administrations and policies before them.

These findings complicate the notion of a Supreme Court uniformly committed to strong presidential power. Executive authority receives substantial protection, but that protection varies with the legal issue, the government’s procedural position, and the particular justices deciding the case. The more revealing question may therefore be which exercises of presidential power command the Court’s support, and which justices are willing to depart from their usual alignments when those powers are tested.

text:
Federal agents raided Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home before dawn on Monday, October 12, 2026, as part of an investigation into possible immigration fraud, just 22 days before the Minnesota congresswoman faces reelection.

Agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, executed a search warrant secured by federal prosecutors. The Justice Department confirmed the operation was part of an ongoing criminal investigation.

The inquiry reportedly centers on documents completed by Omar's late father when she was a child, following the family's flight from Somalia to seek refuge in the United States. Born in Mogadishu, Omar arrived in the country as a refugee in the 1990s and became a naturalized American citizen in 2000.

White House border czar Tom Homan acknowledged an ongoing criminal investigation involving Omar in September, saying immigration authorities were examining allegations that had previously surfaced. The congresswoman said at the time that federal investigators had not contacted her.

Vice President JD Vance had also called for authorities to examine allegations concerning Omar's immigration history and pursue charges if investigators uncovered evidence of wrongdoing. Omar has repeatedly denied accusations of immigration fraud and described claims involving her citizenship and family relationships as politically motivated.

Federal prosecutors obtained judicial authorization for Monday's search, requiring a judge to find probable cause that evidence of a crime would be discovered at the residence. The warrant permitted agents to search for specified materials, although Omar has not been charged in connection with the investigation. The supporting documents remain undisclosed, leaving the precise scope of the search unclear.

Prosecutors seeking a warrant involving a sitting member of Congress also face additional Justice Department oversight. Under Section 9-85.110 of the department's Justice Manual, they must obtain approval from the Public Integrity Section before applying for a warrant covering a lawmaker's property. The provision also requires elevated review within the prosecuting office, with U.S. Attorney approval required where Public Integrity Section approval is necessary.

The additional review applies independently of a judge's determination of probable cause. It requires prosecutors to obtain internal authorization before pursuing certain investigative measures involving members of Congress, including searches of their property or records.

Omar's home was searched 22 days before the November 3 midterm elections, when she is seeking another term representing Minnesota's 5th Congressional District. Under Section 9-85.500 of the Justice Manual, federal prosecutors and agents are prohibited from timing investigative actions to influence an election or benefit a candidate or political party.

The policy also requires consultation with the Public Integrity Section when an investigative step could raise concerns about electoral interference. Federal investigations may proceed during campaign periods, but the timing of those actions must be based on legitimate law enforcement considerations.

The raid drew criticism from congressional Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who accused the Trump administration of using federal law enforcement against political opponents. The search also comes after years of public disputes between Omar and President Donald Trump over immigration enforcement and allegations concerning her background.
